p.seg: The chapter on impermanence teaches that desires can cloud the mind and disrupt it, glory and life are hard to preserve, only the Way is
true.
Upon waking from sleep,
one should joyfully reflect,
listen to what I say,
and record the Buddha's words.
All phenomena are impermanent,
subject to rise and fall;
whatever is born will die,
and extinction brings peace.
Like a potter's vessels,
molded from clay,
all must break;
so too human life.
As a river's swift flow
never returns,
so human life passes—
the gone never come back.
Like a herdsman with staff
grazing cattle,
aging and death
herd life toward its end.
Countless are the clans,
men and women,
hoarding wealth,
yet all must decline and perish.
Day and night, the living
see life whittled away,
lifespan dwindling
like a pond drying up.
The eternal ends,
the lofty falls,
meetings part,
the living die.
Beings contend,
losing their lives;
as their deeds lead,
they reap fortune or calamity.
Age brings suffering,
death severs consciousness;
homes are prisons,
yet greed for the world persists.
Alas, old age arrives,
beauty fades to decay;
youth's vigor
yields to age's trampling.
Though one live a hundred years,
death still takes all;
harassed by aging,
sickness looms near.
Each day that passes
shortens life,
like fish in dwindling water—
what joy is there?
Age withers the form,
sickness corrupts it,
the body rots,
death comes naturally.
What use is this body?
A leaking, foul place,
beset by illness,
plagued by age and death.
Indulging desires,
multiplying wrongs,
blind to change,
one ignores life's impermanence.
No child can save you,
nor parent or sibling;
pressed by death,
no kin offers refuge.
Idling day and night,
aging yet lustful,
hoarding wealth, not giving,
rejecting the Buddha's words—
these four faults
bring self-betrayal.
Not in the sky, nor in the ocean's deep,
Nor in a mountain cave, however steep,
No place exists on earth where one can keep
From death's embrace, no refuge from the leap.
This is the task that I have set to do,
To bring this truth to light and make it true.
People are troubled, restless in their quest,
Treading the path of aging and death's unrest.
Knowing this, one purifies the soul,
Thus seeing the end of birth as the goal.
The bhikkhu, weary of Māra's array,
Crosses beyond the round of birth and decay.
The chapter on teaching guides one's conduct with its precepts, dispelling one's own ignorance and folly, allowing one to
perceive the path with clarity.
Alas! Why do you sleep?
Like worms, snails, and moths,
Concealed in filth and impurity,
Deluded into considering it the body.
How can one be wounded,
With a heart aching like a child's illness,
Facing numerous calamities,
Yet still indulge in sleep?
Reflect and be vigilant,
Practice benevolence and follow its path,
From this, there will be no sorrow,
Constantly mindful of self-restraint.
Cultivate right view and increase learning,
This is the light of the world,
The blessings born from it are a thousandfold,
Never falling into evil paths.
Do not study trivial paths,
lest you believe in wrong views,
do not practice recklessness,
which increases desires;
cultivate good conduct in the Dharma,
learn and recite without transgression,
practice the path without sorrow,
and be constantly at peace through all lifetimes.
Diligently learn to restrain the body,
always be cautious in thought and speech,
for this leads to the deathless,
where practice extinguishes and peace is attained.
Do not study what is unnecessary,
but practice what is essential,
knowing what is worthy of mindfulness,
then the defilements can be extinguished.
Seeing the Dharma benefits the self,
one reaches the good shore,
knowing the benefit of steadfast practice,
this is called wisdom and clarity.
Arising to realize the meaning,
study extinction to become firm,
abide in extinction with self-mastery,
diminish and do not let it arise.
Thus directed, one becomes strong,
in this study, one attains the middle way,
from this, understanding the meaning,
one should remember and practice accordingly.
First, learn to cut off the mother,
lead the ruler and two ministers,
abandon all followers,
this is the superior practitioner.
If study lacks companions,
and no good friends are found,
rather alone uphold goodness,
than accompany the foolish.
Delighting in precepts and study,
what use is a companion?
Alone in goodness, without worry,
like a wild elephant in an open field.
Both precepts and learning are good,
which of the two is superior?
Precepts are praised alongside learning,
one should truly study and practice.
First, in study, protect the precepts,
opening and closing must be firm,
give without receiving,
strive diligently, do not be indolent.
If a man lives a hundred years,
Engaged in evil learning with unwholesome intent,
It is not as good as living a single day,
Diligently pursuing the true Dharma.
If a man lives a hundred years,
Worshipping fire and practicing heterodox arts,
It is not as good as a moment's time,
Devoted to precepts, whose merit is praised.
If one can act, then speak of it;
If not, do not engage in empty talk.
Deceit and lack of sincerity
Are rejected by the wise.
In learning, one should first seek understanding,
Observe and distinguish right from wrong.
Accept the truth and instruct others accordingly;
With wisdom, one is no longer confused.
Those with disheveled hair studying heretical paths,
Clad in grass robes yet inwardly greedy and corrupt,
Blurred and unaware of the truth,
Are like the deaf listening to the five tones.
Learning can help abandon the three evils,
Like medicine that counteracts all poisons.
The strong one crosses over birth and death,
As a snake sheds its old skin.
Learn and be widely informed,
maintain precepts without fail,
receive praise in both worlds,
and achieve what one desires;
learn but be poorly informed,
maintain precepts incompletely,
suffer pain in both worlds,
and lose one's original aspirations.
Now, there are two aspects to learning:
constantly associating with the well-informed,
calmly and attentively understanding the meaning,
even when distressed, not straying into error.
Weeds harm the grain,
excessive desires hinder learning,
uproot all evils,
and the harvest will surely be abundant.
Reflect before speaking,
let words not be forceful or domineering,
expound the Dharma and its principles,
so that none may contradict.
He who learns well commits no offenses,
reveres the law and understands taboos,
sees the subtle and knows the implications,
cautious, he avoids future troubles.
Keep far from sin and blessings,
strive to accomplish the holy life,
restrain oneself throughout life,
this is called true learning.
The Chapter on Extensive Learning encourages the pursuit of knowledge, for accumulating understanding leads to sagehood, naturally attaining the right
enlightenment.
Extensive learning enables steadfast retention,
Upholding the Dharma as a protective wall,
Diligence is hard to breach or destroy,
From this, precepts and wisdom are perfected;
Extensive learning clarifies the will,
Once clarified, wisdom increases,
Wisdom then broadly comprehends meanings,
Understanding meanings, one practices the Dharma in peace;
Extensive learning can dispel sorrow,
Able to find joy in concentration,
Skillfully expounding the nectarous Dharma,
One attains Nirvāṇa by oneself.
Learning leads to knowing the Dharma and its principles,
Resolving doubts and perceiving truth,
Through learning, one abandons the unrighteous,
Progressing to the deathless state.
Able to demonstrate the path as a teacher,
Resolving doubts to enlighten learners,
Also reviving the root of purity,
Capable of preserving the Dharma treasury.
Able to grasp and understand meanings,
Understanding prevents misinterpretation,
Those who receive and rely on the Dharma,
From this swiftly attain peace.
If one has but little learning,
And grows arrogant, scorning others,
This is like a blind man holding a torch,
Illuminating others but not himself.
Seeking rank, wealth,
Honor, or heavenly blessings,
Eloquence, wisdom, or worldly prowess—
Such learning is foremost.
Kings court learning with reverence,
So too do the heavens and celestial beings,
Learning is the supreme treasure,
The richest, with the strongest vigor.
The wise yield to learning,
Those who love the Way also delight in it,
Rulers serve it wholeheartedly,
Even Śakra and Brahmā do the same.
Sages always revere learning,
How much more the noble and wealthy?
Thus, wisdom is most precious,
Nothing surpasses it in worthiness of respect.
Serve the sun for its light,
Serve the father for his kindness,
Serve the ruler with strength,
Serve the learned for the Way.
One serves a doctor for life's sake,
Relies on the mighty to overcome,
The Dharma resides in wisdom's place,
Meritorious deeds bring clarity across lifetimes.
Observe friends in times of planning,
Distinguish companions in urgency;
Watch a wife in domestic joy,
Know wisdom through discourse.
Learning benefits this present life,
For wife, children, brothers, and friends,
It also secures future blessings,
Accumulated learning forms sagely wisdom.
It can disperse sorrow and anger,
Also remove misfortune and decline,
To gain safety and auspiciousness,
One should serve the learned.
No wound cuts deeper than grief,
No arrow pierces sharper than folly,
This strength none can uproot,
Only through extensive learning is it removed.
The blind gain sight from it,
The dark gain a torch from it,
It also guides the people of the world,
Like eyes for the eyeless.
Therefore, discard ignorance,
Abandon pride, embrace noble wealth's joy,
Diligently study and serve the learned,
This is called accumulating virtue.
The chapter on Steadfast Faith is the root of establishing the Way, where the fruit lies in the cause of right view, and actions do not
look back.
Faith shames the mind that covets wealth,
This Dharma is praised by noble scholars,
This path is spoken by the wise and discerning,
Thus one ascends to the heavenly realm.
Fools do not cultivate heavenly conduct,
Nor do they praise generosity,
But faithful giving aids the virtuous,
From this, they reach that peace.
The faithful grow as true persons,
Dwelling securely in mindfulness of the Dharma;
The diligent attain higher states of mind,
The wise, in longevity, excel among the long-lived.
Faith can attain the Way,
the Dharma leads to extinction and liberation,
from listening, wisdom is gained,
wherever one arrives, there is clarity;
faith can cross the abyss,
grasping it makes one a shipmaster,
diligence removes suffering,
wisdom reaches the other shore.
A person with faithful conduct,
is praised by the sages,
those who delight in non-action,
all bonds are untied.
Faith and precepts,
the wise mind can practice,
the strong overcome anger,
from this, they escape the abyss.
Faith enables precepts to be sincere,
and also receives wisdom,
able to practice everywhere,
nourished in every place.
Compared to worldly gains,
wise faith is the light,
it is the supreme treasure of wealth,
an extraordinary family asset.
Wishing to see all truths,
delighting in hearing the teachings,
able to abandon stinginess and defilements,
this is what faith is.
Faith can cross the river,
its blessings cannot be taken away,
it can stop theft,
the joy of wilderness ascetics.
Without faith, one does not learn,
fond of distorting right speech,
like clumsily fetching water,
digging a spring and stirring up mud.
The wise practice wisdom,
delighting in clear streams,
like skillfully drawing water,
thinking to avoid disturbance.
Faith does not taint others,
only the virtuous and humane,
what is good, then learn;
what is not good, then avoid.
Faith is my carriage,
none know its load,
like a tamed elephant,
self-taming is the supreme.
Faith wealth, precept wealth,
shame, remorse also wealth,
hearing wealth, giving wealth,
wisdom is the seventh wealth.
From faith, uphold precepts,
constantly observe the Dharma purely,
wisely and beneficially act,
reverently serve without forgetting.
Born with these treasures,
regardless of man or woman,
ultimately never poor,
the wise recognize the truth.
The chapter on vigilance and caution teaches the bestowal of virtuous paths and the prohibition of wicked wrongs, so that there may be no
regrets thereafter.
One who is constantly pure,
upholds the precepts till the end,
cultivates good deeds with purity,
thus completes the discipline.
The wise guard the precepts,
their blessings lead to the Three Jewels,
gaining fame and benefits,
and later ascending to heavenly bliss.
Always dwelling in the Dharma,
guarding the precepts as light,
they attain true insight,
and become auspicious among their peers.
The disciplined one is at peace,
free from bodily afflictions,
sleeps tranquilly at night,
and awakens with constant joy.
Cultivate precepts and generosity,
perform merits for blessings,
from here to there,
always reaching a place of peace.
What end is good?
What good brings peace?
What is the treasure for humans?
What theft does not take?
Discipline brings peace in old age,
discipline is the good that brings peace,
wisdom is the human treasure,
blessings are what thieves cannot take.
A bhikṣu establishes discipline,
guards and restrains the senses,
eats with self-control,
and awakens the mind to responsiveness.
With discipline, subdue the mind,
maintain right concentration of thought,
inwardly learn right contemplation,
never forgetting right wisdom.
The wise guard the precepts,
inwardly reflect on right wisdom,
practice the path as appropriate,
purify themselves and remove suffering.
Eliminate all defilements,
eradicate pride and prevent its arising,
seek the Dharma throughout life,
never briefly stray from the sage.
Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—
these should be well contemplated,
having already removed defilements,
free from calamities, eliminating existence.
With understanding, one crosses over,
no further rebirth occurs,
transcending all demon realms,
clear as the bright sun.
Wild delusion and self-indulgence—
always avoid them outwardly,
precepts, concentration, and wisdom practices—
seek their fulfillment without departing.
Maintaining pure discipline,
the mind does not indulge itself,
with right wisdom attained,
one no longer beholds wrong paths.
This leads to an auspicious place,
for the supreme way,
also abandoning the wrong path,
leaving all demon realms behind.
The chapter on mindfulness is the beginning of preserving subtlety; within, contemplating the breath, one must comprehend the principles of the Way.
Mindfulness of in-breath and out-breath,
fully endowed with contemplation of truth,
from beginning to end, thoroughly mastered,
peaceful as the Buddha taught.
This illuminates the world,
like clouds clearing to reveal the moon;
arising and ceasing, learning to contemplate,
sitting or lying down, never neglecting.
A bhikṣu establishing this mindfulness,
early benefits, later excels,
starting well, ending victoriously,
passing beyond, no longer seeing birth and death.
If one sees the abode of the body,
the six senses as foremost,
a bhikṣu constantly single-minded,
then knows Nirvāṇa by oneself.
Having these various mindfulnesses,
constantly building up one's own practice,
if one does not do so,
will never attain the intended path.
This is following the fundamental practice,
thus crossing over the toil of craving;
if able to awaken the mindful intent,
knowing the joy of single-mindedness.
Timely practicing the equal Dharma,
this crosses over the distress of aging and death;
a bhikṣu awakening the intentional actions,
should maintain this mindfulness.
All thoughts of birth and death abandoned,
able to make an end of suffering;
constantly should listen to the subtle,
awakening one's own mind.
One who can awaken is virtuous,
from start to finish, nothing clung to;
with awakened mind able to respond,
day and night diligently learning and practicing,
should understand the essence of nectar,
causing all defilements to be exhausted.
A person who gains wholesome benefits,
comes to take refuge in the Buddha;
therefore, day and night,
constantly recollect the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Knowing and awakening one's own mind,
this is a disciple of the Buddha;
constantly day and night recollecting,
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Recollecting the body, impermanence,
recollecting precepts, the virtue of giving,
emptiness, wishlessness, signlessness—
day and night should recollect these.
The Chapter on Compassion and Benevolence, this refers to the path trodden by great individuals and sages, whose virtue is universal and immeasurably
boundless.
To be benevolent and refrain from killing,
constantly able to guard one's body,
is to dwell in immortality,
and wherever one goes, there is no harm;
refraining from killing is benevolence,
being cautious in speech and guarding the mind,
is to dwell in immortality,
and wherever one goes, there is no harm.
When chaos has been ordered,
maintain it with compassionate benevolence,
able to endure when faced with anger,
this is the practice of Brahmacarya;
sincere, calm, and unhurried,
with no harsh words from the mouth,
not angered by others' actions,
this is called the practice of Brahmacarya;
ruling effortlessly through non-action,
harming no living beings,
causing no disturbance or trouble,
this is the response of Brahmacarya.
Constantly with compassionate sorrow,
pure as the Buddha's teaching,
knowing contentment and knowing when to stop,
this is to cross over birth and death.
Having few desires and a love for learning,
not deluded by profit,
benevolent and without offense,
praised by the world.
Benevolent and long-lived without offense,
not giving rise to change or haste,
when others engage in disputes and disturbances,
the wise remain silent and peaceful.
Universally concerned for virtuous friends,
sorrowful for all living beings,
constantly practicing a compassionate heart,
wherever one goes, there is peace.
Benevolent and scholarly, not deviant,
dwelling peacefully without worry,
protected by heaven;
the wise delight in compassion,
day and night mindful of compassion,
the heart without contention or aggression,
harming no living beings.
This conduct holds no enmity,
without compassion, there is killing,
violating precepts and speaking falsely,
faults not passed to others.
Not observing living beings,
wine leads to loss of will,
engaging in reckless behavior,
later falling into evil paths.
Without sincerity, there is no truth,
walking in benevolence and practicing compassion,
loving broadly and aiding the masses,
brings eleven praises:
fortune always follows the person,
sleeping peacefully, waking peacefully,
not seeing evil dreams,
protected by heaven, loved by people,
not poisoned, not harmed by weapons,
not perishing by water or fire,
gaining profit wherever one is,
upon death ascending to the Brahma heaven,
these are the eleven.
If mindful of compassionate heart,
immeasurable and unceasing,
birth and death gradually lessen,
gaining benefit and transcending the world.
Benevolence brings no disordered will,
compassion is the most practicable,
pitying and grieving for living beings,
this fortune is immeasurable.
Even if one were to exhaust their lifespan,
Diligently serving all people under heaven,
And offering elephants and horses in sacrifice to the heavens,
It would not compare to performing a single act of compassion.
The chapter on speech serves to warn the mouth; when expressing opinions and engaging in discussions, one should employ the principles of the Way.
Uttering harsh words and insults,
arrogantly despising others,
giving rise to such conduct,
breeds resentment and animosity;
With gentle speech and compliant words,
showing respect to others,
abandoning grudges and enduring malice,
resentment and animosity vanish on their own.
In the life of a person,
an axe lies within the mouth,
which can wound the self,
through its harmful words.
Strife yields little benefit,
as if covering up lost wealth,
following it leads to contention,
causing intentions to turn toward evil.
Praising the wicked and denouncing the praiseworthy,
both are evil deeds.
Those fond of verbal disputes,
will ultimately find no peace.
Without righteousness, one falls into evil paths,
increasing their own hellish sufferings.
Stay away from foolishness, cultivate a patient mind,
contemplate truth to avoid transgression.
Through goodness, liberation is attained;
through evil, no release is found.
Those who understand goodness are wise—
this is freedom from afflictions.
Embrace self-restraint in understanding,
speak without haste, finding the middle way.
Speak rightly, speak in accordance with Dharma,
such words are gentle and sweet.
Therefore, in speech,
one must ensure they cause themselves no harm,
nor overpower others—
this is skillful speech.
Let words meet others’ intentions appropriately,
and bring them joy,
not leading to ill will,
so that all accept what is spoken.
Sincere words are like nectar,
in accordance with Dharma and without fault.
Truthful, righteous, and lawful—
this is to stand near the Path.
Those who speak as the Buddha taught
are blessed and attain Nirvāṇa,
able to reach the far shore—
this is called the highest speech.
The chapter "Dual Essentials" elucidates through pairs, where good and evil are contrasted, presenting meanings not in isolation.
The mind is the root of all phenomena,
the mind is sovereign, the mind governs;
if the mind harbors evil thoughts,
words and actions follow,
suffering and sin pursue one of their own accord,
as the wheel follows the hoof-print of the ox.
The mind is the root of all things,
it is noble and commanding.
If the heart thinks of goodness,
then words and actions follow,
happiness and blessings naturally pursue,
like a shadow following the body.
Following confused thoughts leads astray,
Embracing ignorance plunges into darkness,
Arrogance leaves no room for discipline,
How can one understand good counsel?
Follow the path of righteousness,
with understanding clear and bright,
free from envy and jealousy,
adept at wise words.
Those who harbor anger over grievances,
have never been without grievances;
by not harboring anger, they naturally dissipate,
this is the Way that can be revered.
Do not readily blame others,
but strive to examine yourself.
If one understands this principle,
troubles will vanish forever without distress.
One who acts seeing the purity of the body,
yet does not restrain the senses,
eats and drinks without moderation,
is indolent, negligent, and cowardly,
will be controlled by evil influences,
as the wind bends down the grass;
Contemplate the body as impure,
to restrain all senses,
eat with moderation,
always delight in diligence,
unmoved by evil influences,
like a great mountain against the wind.
Without purging the venomous disposition,
desires run wild,
unable to self-regulate,
one is unworthy of the Dharma robe;
Capable of expelling venomous states,
with disciplined thoughts remaining tranquil,
a subdued mind already tamed,
this befits the Dharma robe.
Taking the true as false and
the false as true,
this is a deceitful scheme,
yielding no true benefit;
To recognize truth as truth,
to see falsehood as falsehood,
this is right discernment,
and surely brings true benefit.
If a house is not tightly built,
when it rains, it will leak;
if intentions are not focused,
excesses will create breaches.
Build a house well and tightly,
and when it rains, it won't leak.
Control your thoughts and focus on action,
and improper desires will not arise.
When a lowly person influences others,
it is like approaching foul objects;
gradually, they become accustomed to wrongdoing,
unaware that they have turned evil.
A virtuous man influences others,
As if being near fragrant incense,
He advances wisdom and practices goodness,
His conduct becomes pure and fragrant.
Creating worries leads to future worries,
Committing evil deeds brings twofold anxieties,
Those worries are but fears,
Seeing one's faults, the heart trembles with dread;
Creating joy brings subsequent delight,
Performing good deeds yields twofold happiness,
That joy alone brings true merriment,
Seeing blessings brings peace to the heart;
Regret now and regret later,
For the evil done, twice the remorse,
Such actions bring their own calamity,
Suffering torment and scorching distress;
Joy now and joy hereafter,
Doing good brings twofold joy,
Thus one secures self-blessing,
Receiving fortune, delight and ease.
Skilled in flattery and full of demands,
unrestrained and without discipline,
harboring lust, anger, and delusion,
not contemplating cessation and insight,
gathering like a herd of cattle—
such are not disciples of the Buddha.
At times, speak with few desires,
practice the Way in accordance with the Dharma,
eliminate lust, anger, and ignorance,
awaken to right mindfulness and understanding,
see without opposition,
this is a disciple of the Buddha.
The Chapter on Dissipation,
draws on discipline to restrain desires,
guards against deviance and corrects faults,
urging the virtuous with the Way.
Restraint is the path to nectar-like enlightenment,
Negligence is the road to death;
By not clinging, one escapes mortality,
Losing the Way brings self-destruction;
The wise who guard the Way triumph,
Never indulging in negligence,
Not craving, they attain joy,
And from this gain the bliss of the Way.
Always be mindful of the Way,
Strengthen yourself and uphold righteousness in action;
The vigorous will attain salvation in this world,
Auspiciousness knows no greater state.
With constant mindfulness arising,
Practicing purity, evil easily fades away,
Self-restraint leads to a life of Dharma,
Without transgression, good reputation grows.
Issue without negligence,
Restrain to regulate the mind oneself,
Wisdom can create the clarity of concentration,
Never to return to the abyss of darkness.
The foolish are hard to enlighten,
Greedy for chaos and fond of disputes;
The wise are ever cautious and prudent,
Guarding this as a precious treasure.
Do not covet, do not delight in contention,
nor indulge in sensual pleasures,
with a mindful heart free from negligence,
one can attain great peace.
To curb one's own indulgence is self-restraint,
He who can repel it is a worthy man,
Having ascended the tower of wisdom,
Leaving danger, one finds immediate safety.
The wise observe the foolish,
As a mountain overlooks the plain.
To remain upright amidst chaos,
One alone attains enlightenment,
Such strength surpasses that of a lion,
Abandoning evil is the greatest wisdom.
Sleep is heavy as a mountain,
Ignorance obscures the mind,
Lying in comfort, unaware of suffering,
Thus one is constantly reborn.
Not indulging freely at any time,
One can control and exhaust the outflows.
Indulging freely, Māra gains advantage,
Like a lion pouncing on a deer.
One who can refrain from self-indulgence,
is a disciplined monk;
those who contemplate purity and righteousness
should always guard their own minds.
The bhikkhu who is cautious finds happiness,
While the negligent are filled with sorrow and distress.
From minor disputes, great conflicts arise,
And accumulated wrongdoings lead one into the flames.
By upholding precepts, blessings arrive and goodness is attained,
by violating precepts, a fearful heart arises,
one can sever the outflows of the three realms,
this is to approach Nirvāṇa.
If one was reckless before,
but later can restrain oneself,
this illuminates the world,
with mindfulness establishing what is proper;
To err is human evil,
but to amend with good deeds,
this illuminates the world,
cherishing goodness as the right path.
In youth, he left home,
devoutly practiced the Buddhist teachings,
illuminating the world,
like the moon clearing the clouds;
One who does evil in front of others,
but later stops and does not repeat it,
illuminates the world,
like the moon when clouds disperse.
Living without causing distress,
dying without sorrow,
this is the valor of seeing the Way,
one should not grieve in between.
To sever the turbid and dark methods,
learning solely pursues purity and clarity,
crossing the abyss without turning back,
abandoning attachments in action and rest,
no longer indulging in defiling pleasures,
desiring to cut off worries and be free from sorrow.
The spirit of intention,
though empty and formless,
creates without exhaustion.
If one acts like a dog,
it becomes hard to protect and restrain;
when wisdom corrects the root,
its clarity becomes great.
Lightness and impatience are hard to maintain,
only desires are followed,
mastering the mind leads to goodness,
self-discipline brings peace.
Subtle thoughts are hard to perceive,
Following desires wherever they lead,
Wisdom constantly guards itself,
He who can preserve it finds peace.
Walking alone far into the distance,
concealing oneself without a trace,
diminishing desires to approach the Way,
then the demons' bonds are loosened.
The mind does not abide or rest,
nor does it know the Dharma,
it is confused by worldly affairs,
and lacks correct wisdom.
Thoughts have no fixed end,
unceasing and boundless,
virtue can restrain evil,
the awakened are deemed wise.
The Buddha teaches the mind's dharma,
though subtle, it is not the ultimate truth;
one should awaken to wandering thoughts,
and not follow a distracted heart.
Seeing the Dharma brings the greatest peace,
all wishes are fulfilled,
wisdom protects subtle intentions,
severing the causes and conditions of suffering.
This body will not last long,
All must return to the earth;
When the form decays and the spirit departs,
What is there to covet in this temporary abode?
When the heart anticipates creating situations,
coming and going without clear reason,
thoughts often turn deviant and corrupt,
one brings misfortune upon oneself.
This intention is self-made,
Not given by parents' hand,
Strive to walk the righteous path,
Do not turn from blessings' stand.
Conceal the six senses like a tortoise,
Guard the mind like a fortress,
Let wisdom battle demons,
Victory ensures no distress.
The study should be practical,
revealing the essence through its splendor,
and turning falsehood back into truth.
Who can choose a place,
Forsaking the mirror to grasp the heavens?
Who speaks the Dharma verses,
As if selecting the finest blossoms?
Scholars choose their ground,
Forsaking the mirror to grasp the heavens;
Skillfully expounding the Dharma verses,
They can gather the blossoms of virtue.
Knowing the world's decay as a metaphor,
illusory dharmas suddenly appear,
cutting off demons, flowers bloom,
without beholding birth and death;
See the body as foam,
illusory dharmas arise spontaneously,
sever demons, flowers bloom,
without beholding birth and death.
When the body is ill, it withers,
Like blossoms falling and scattering;
When the final summons arrives,
It is as swift as rushing waters.
Insatiable greed,
dissipates one's resolve,
wealth obtained through wicked means,
brings self-deception and harm.
Like bees gathering on flowers,
not harming their colors or fragrance,
but only taking the flavor away,
so the benevolent enter a gathering.
Do not focus on observing others,
whether they act or not,
but constantly examine yourself,
to know what is right and what is not.
Like a pleasing flower,
Beautiful in color but without fragrance,
So is eloquent speech
That is not put into practice—it yields no reward.
Like a delightful flower,
beautiful in color and fragrant,
one who speaks skillfully and acts virtuously
will surely attain blessings.
Make many precious flowers,
weave hairpins with dangling ornaments,
those who accumulate abundant virtue,
will be reborn in better circumstances.
Exotic grasses and fragrant flowers,
do not defy the wind's fragrance,
blossom near the path,
their virtue draws others to their scent.
Sandalwood has much fragrance,
Blue lotuses bear fragrant flowers,
Though these are indeed real,
They are not as good as the fragrance of precepts.
The fragrance of flowers is faint and subtle,
it cannot be called true;
the fragrance of upholding precepts,
reaches the heavens with unparalleled excellence.
With precepts perfected,
practice without negligence,
concentrate the mind to attain liberation,
long depart from the demon's path.
Like a field ditch,
close to the main road,
lotus flowers grow in it,
fragrant, pure, and pleasing to the mind.
There is birth and death indeed,
ordinary people dwell on the edge,
the wise delight in transcending it,
becoming disciples of the Buddha.
To enlighten the ignorant,
I thus present the forms,
So they may glimpse the light.
Sleepless, the night is long;
weary, the road is long;
ignorant, the cycle of birth and death is long,
for they know not the true Dharma.
Foolish thoughts often sink into obscurity,
Passing like a flowing stream,
Persisting in a single path with effort,
Alone and without a companion.
The foolish cling to their schemes,
worry and sorrow linger long.
To dwell with fools is suffering;
they hold grievances against me.
With sons and wealth,
the fool toils anxiously,
but if I am not even myself,
why worry about sons and wealth?
In summer, one should stop here;
in winter, one should stop here.
The foolish are full of worries,
unaware of what changes may come.
The foolish and ignorant, in their extreme folly,
Consider themselves wise,
Yet folly triumphs over wisdom,
This is called the height of foolishness.
The stubborn and dim-witted approaching wisdom,
is like ladling flavors with a gourd,
though long familiar and accustomed,
still remain unaware of the principles.
To open up and approach the wise,
is like the tongue tasting flavors;
though practiced for only a moment,
one immediately grasps the essence of the Way.
A fool's actions,
bring calamity upon himself;
taking pleasure in wrongdoing,
he brings grave disaster upon his own head.
When one commits an unwholesome deed,
and later feels regret and remorse,
leading to tears streaming down the face,
it is the result of past habits;
Act with virtuous goodness,
Advance to behold joy,
Should come to receive blessings,
Laughing happily and delighting in practice.
When the offense is not yet ripe,
the fool thinks it is calm and peaceful,
but when it reaches its ripeness,
they themselves suffer great punishment.
Where I had hoped to go,
I did not think it would bring suffering;
only when facing the brink of calamity,
did I realize it was unwise.
The foolish commit evil deeds,
unable to free themselves,
disaster pursues and engulfs them,
their sins blaze into fierce flames.
I am fond of fine food,
and this indulgence grows greater with each passing month.
Out of every sixteen parts of my thoughts,
not one is devoted to the Dharma.
The ignorant student's thoughts and concerns,
Ultimately lead to no benefit,
Bringing upon oneself the blade and staff,
Retribution bearing the seal of authority.
Observing their actions reveals their folly,
They seek widely without giving,
Fallen from the path of wisdom,
Often engaging in wicked deeds.
Those who seek distant goals over immediate desires,
study for the sake of knowledge rather than food,
and refrain from greedily clinging to family comforts,
often provide for others beyond their own kin.
In learning, do not fall into expectations,
do not become a household monk,
for greed violates the sacred teachings,
leading to future scarcity for oneself.
This journey is the same as that of the foolish,
but it causes desires and arrogance to increase,
the aspirations for seeking benefits differ,
and the intentions for seeking the Way also differ.
Therefore, those with awareness,
emerge as disciples of the Buddha,
abandon attachments and forsake worldly habits,
and ultimately do not fall into the cycle of life and death.
The Chapter on Wisdom,
presents the practice of the wise,
cultivating blessings and advancing on the path,
with the Dharma as a clear mirror.
Deeply observe good and evil,
know in your heart to fear and be cautious,
fear and do not transgress,
ultimately auspicious and free from worry.
Thus, the world has blessings,
reflecting on continuing virtuous deeds,
skillfully achieving one's aspirations,
fortune and prosperity grow ever greater.
Believe that doing good brings blessings,
Accumulate virtuous deeds without wearying,
Trust in the knowledge of hidden virtues,
In time, they will surely shine forth.
Always avoid what is without righteousness,
do not associate with foolish people,
think of following virtuous friends,
and stay close to superior scholars.
Delighting in the Dharma brings peaceful rest,
The heart rejoices and the mind is clear,
The sage expounds the teachings,
Wisdom constantly leads to joyful practice.
The benevolent and the wise,
observe abstinence and uphold the Way,
like the moon among the stars,
illuminating the world.
The bow-maker adjusts the horn,
the boatman adjusts the vessel,
the carpenter adjusts the wood,
the wise person adjusts themselves.
Like a solid rock,
unmoved by the wind,
the wise hold firm convictions,
unswayed by praise or blame;
Like a deep abyss,
clear and serene,
the wise one hears the truth,
with a purified heart, rejoicing.
The great man embodies desirelessness,
His clarity illuminates all he encounters;
Though he may face suffering or joy,
He does not flaunt his wisdom.
The great sage is unconcerned with worldly affairs,
Desiring neither sons nor wealth nor state,
Constantly upholding the path of precepts and wisdom,
Coveting not unrighteous riches or honors.
The wise know the wavering mind,
Like a tree in the shifting sand,
When a friend's resolve is not firm,
Their nature is dyed by the colors around.
The world is submerged in deep waters,
few can reach the shore.
If there is someone,
desiring to cross, they must strive.
Those who truly desire the Path,
receive and study the true teachings,
this draws near the other shore,
transcending death is paramount.
The method to sever the five aggregates,
calmly contemplate wisdom,
do not return to enter the abyss,
abandon reliance on one's clarity.
Restrain desires and passions,
Abandon pleasures and practice non-action,
One can thereby save and aid oneself,
Making the mind attain wisdom.
Learn to acquire correct wisdom,
Focus the mind solely on the right path,
With undivided heart accept the truth,
Find joy in non-arising,
Exhaust the outflows and eliminate the habits,
Thus one attains liberation in the world.
The Chapter on Arhats,
speaks of the true nature of a person
freeing themselves from desires, unattached,
with a heart unwavering and unchanged.
Having left behind sorrows and afflictions,
freed from all bonds,
the knots of entanglement untied,
cool and without warmth.
With a purified mind, one attains mindfulness,
free from any greed or attachment,
having crossed the abyss of ignorance,
like a wild goose abandoning the pond.
Eat according to one's capacity,
with no hoarded stores,
the mind empty and free of thoughts,
guiding all beings through their paths.
Like a bird in the sky,
it flies far away without hindrance.
All worldly habits exhausted,
no longer relying on others for sustenance.
With an empty heart free from troubles,
having reached the place of liberation,
like a flying bird,
briefly alighting then swiftly departing.
Control the roots and follow restraint,
Like a horse well-tamed and disciplined,
Abandon the habits of pride and arrogance,
To be revered by the heavens.
Unangered like the earth,
unshaken like a mountain,
the true person is without defilement,
transcending the cycle of life and death.
The mind has come to rest,
words and deeds are also upright,
liberated through righteousness,
peacefully returning to extinction.
Abandoning desires without attachment,
rid of the three realms' hindrances,
with aspirations already severed,
this is called a superior person.
At the gathering in Ruòyě,
on level ground and high banks,
where the Arhats passed by,
all were blessed without exception.
He delights in tranquility,
which ordinary people cannot achieve,
joyful without expectations,
free from all desires.
The chapter on narrating a thousand items
shows learners that having many classics
but lacking essentials
is not as good as being concise and clear.
Though one recites a thousand words,
if the meaning of the sentences is incorrect,
it is not as good as one essential truth,
hearing which can extinguish distracting thoughts;
Though one recites a thousand words,
what benefit is there without righteousness?
Better is a single righteous principle,
hearing and practicing which one may cross to the other shore.
Although one recites many scriptures,
what benefit is there without understanding?
Understanding a single phrase of the Dharma,
and practicing it, one can attain the Way.
To overcome a thousand enemies,
Is achieved by one man's might;
Yet better still is self-conquest,
The supreme victory in the fight.
To conquer oneself is the greatest excellence,
hence it is said to be the hero among men,
guarding the mind and disciplining the body,
from self-restraint to the very end.
Although it is said to honor Heaven,
gods, demons, Brahmā, and Indra
are none able to surpass
the one who has mastered oneself.
Making sacrifices monthly for a thousand years,
and never ceasing throughout one's life,
is not as good as a single moment,
with a focused mind contemplating the Dharma.
One thought of the Way's blessings
surpasses a lifetime of those offerings.
Though one may spend a hundred years,
serving the fire sacrifice,
it is not as good as a moment,
devoted to honoring the Three Jewels;
a single act of such devotion brings merit,
surpassing that of a century.
Offer sacrifices to gods seeking blessings,
then observe the outcomes from behind,
finding not even a quarter of hopes met;
it's better to honor the virtuous.
One who is adept at practicing etiquette and propriety,
and consistently respects elders and seniors,
will naturally see four blessings increase:
in complexion, strength, longevity, and peace.
If a person lives a hundred years,
but is far from righteousness and does not uphold precepts,
it is better to live a single day
guarding precepts with right mindfulness and meditation;
If a man lives a hundred years,
devoid of wisdom and steeped in falsehood,
it is better to live a single day
with a mind devoted to true wisdom.
If a person lives a hundred years,
But is idle and not diligent,
It is better to live a single day
Striving with earnest effort.
If a person lives a hundred years,
but remains ignorant of the causes of success and failure,
it is better to live just one day
and discern the subtle signs to know what to avoid.
If a person lives a hundred years,
but does not see the path of immortality,
it is better to live a single day
and taste the flavor of immortality.
If a man lives a hundred years,
but does not know the great truth,
it is better to live for a single day,
and learn the essence of the Buddha's teachings.
The Chapter on Evil Deeds,
profoundly moves evil people
to realize that every action bears sinful retribution,
and that only by refraining from such acts can one be free from calamity.
Seeing goodness yet not following it,
instead indulging in wicked thoughts,
seeking blessings through improper means,
instead delighting in depraved excesses.
When ordinary people commit evil deeds,
they often fail to realize it themselves;
in their foolishness, they find fleeting pleasure,
only to store up bitterness for the future.
The wicked commit atrocities,
Sinking deeper repeatedly,
Craving to act on their desires,
Retribution follows naturally;
The virtuous person practices goodness,
with each act accumulating and increasing,
willingly engaging in it,
and blessings naturally follow.
When evil deeds bear fruit,
their wickedness is not yet ripe.
When their wickedness ripens,
they themselves suffer the punishment.
Auspicious signs appear amidst misfortune,
for goodness has not yet ripened;
when that goodness reaches full maturity,
one is sure to receive its blessings.
He who strikes others will be struck;
he who acts with resentment will receive resentment;
he who insults others will be insulted;
he who shows anger will be met with anger.
People in the world are ignorant,
unaware of the true teachings.
Life is short and fleeting,
why should one choose to do evil?
Do not belittle small evils,
thinking they bring no calamity.
Though a drop of water is tiny,
it gradually fills a large vessel.
All sins, when they abound,
are accumulated from small beginnings.
Do not belittle small acts of goodness,
thinking they bring no blessings.
Though droplets of water are tiny,
they gradually fill a large vessel.
All blessings reach fullness
through accumulation from the slightest beginnings.
A scholar's conduct,
whether liked or disliked,
is for their own self-cultivation,
and will ultimately not lead to ruin.
Those who are fond of taking,
consider themselves justified,
yet those who take from them,
are also justified by others.
Evil not immediately punished,
Is like curdling cow's milk,
Sins hidden in dark shrines,
Are like ashes covering fire.
Taking jest as evil conduct,
thus creating bodily deeds,
one weeps and wails receiving retribution,
as the consequences of actions arrive.
Committing evil without concealment,
like being intercepted by soldiers,
only when dragged away does one realize,
they have already fallen into wicked deeds.
Later, they suffer the retribution,
as they had practiced before.
Like a poisonous festering sore,
a boat caught in a whirlpool,
evil deeds spread and multiply,
leaving nothing unharmed.
To falsely accuse others with malice,
Their purity remains untainted.
The fool's calamity rebounds upon himself,
Like dust blown back by the wind.
To err is not evil,
To repent and do good is,
It illuminates the world,
Like the sun without a clouded cover.
A scholar's conduct,
then becomes manifest in his own person,
doing good brings good,
doing evil brings evil.
Those with consciousness fall into the womb,
The wicked descend into hell,
Those who do good ascend to heaven,
Through non-action, one attains Nirvana.
Not in the void, not in the sea,
nor hidden among mountain rocks,
can one in such places
escape the calamity of past misdeeds.
All beings have sufferings and distress,
Unable to escape aging and death.
Only the benevolent and wise
Do not dwell on others' faults and evils.
The Chapter on Knives and Staves,
teaches to practice benevolence,
and not to wield knives or staves
to harm living beings.
All fear death,
All dread the pain of the rod.
Put oneself in their place:
Do not kill, do not strike.
To often bring peace to all living beings,
Without inflicting suffering upon them,
In this life, one encounters no harm,
And in the afterlife, long dwells in tranquility.
Do not speak harshly,
for words bring fearful retribution;
evil deeds go forth and calamity returns,
with blades and staves descending upon one's body.
To speak with goodness,
is like striking bells and chimes;
with no criticism of one's person,
navigating the world becomes easy.
To beat the good and kind with a cane,
to slander the innocent falsely,
brings calamity tenfold upon oneself,
with swift disaster leaving no pardon:
Enduring excruciating pain;
The body broken and disfigured;
Naturally afflicted with illness;
Disoriented and bewildered in despair;
Slandered and blamed by others;
Or oppressed by government officials;
Wealth and property exhausted;
Relatives and friends parted.
Abandoning all dwellings,
they are consumed by calamitous fires;
and upon death, fall into hell.
Thus are the ten.
Even if one strips to bare skin and cuts off hair,
dons coarse garments for long,
bathes and squats on stones,
what can be done about the knots of foolishness?
Without felling, killing, or burning,
Nor seeking victory,
One cherishes all under heaven,
And wherever one goes, there are no grievances.
In the world, there are those
who can feel shame and remorse;
this is called guidance and improvement,
like spurring a fine horse.
Like a well-trained horse,
it can travel far on the path.
If a person has faith and discipline,
with focused mind and diligent effort,
they will attain wisdom through the Way,
and thus eliminate all sufferings.
He disciplines himself to cultivate the Dharma,
Diminishing desires and purifying conduct,
Never raising a staff against any living being—
Such is the monastic practitioner.
Harmless to the world,
Throughout life, one encounters no harm,
Constantly compassionate toward all,
Who could bear a grudge against them?
The elderly squander their time,
teaching others to toil diligently,
yet not contending with fate—
what use is regret in old age?
What is there to rejoice? What is there to laugh?
Life constantly blazes,
Deeply flawed and obscure,
As if not seeking the lamp.
Seeing the physical form as a model,
Leaning on it for security,
Excessive thoughts lead to illness,
How can one know it is not real?
When old, one's complexion fades,
when ill, it lacks luster,
the skin slackens and muscles shrink,
and death's approach draws near.
When the soul departs and death draws near,
Like a discarded chariot, no longer steered,
The flesh dissolves, the bones scatter wide,
On what can the body then rely with pride?
The body is like a fortress,
With bones as pillars and flesh as plaster,
From birth to old age and death,
It only harbors anger and arrogance.
When one grows old, the body changes,
like an old cart.
The Dharma can eliminate suffering,
so one should diligently study it.
A person who lacks reputation,
grows old like a draft ox,
only gaining muscle and fat,
without any blessings or wisdom.
Life and death are meaningless,
Coming and going are fraught with hardship,
The mind clings greedily to this body,
Life's suffering knows no end.
Wisdom reveals suffering,
thus one abandons the body,
extinguishes the mind and severs actions,
ending desire to attain non-birth.
Neither cultivating the noble practice,
nor amassing wealth,
one grows old like a white egret
guarding an empty pond.
They neither uphold the precepts,
nor accumulate wealth,
growing old and frail until their energy is exhausted—
how can they then pursue their aspirations in time?
Old as autumn leaves,
Why tarnish the mirror's record?
When fate swiftly arrives,
Regret then is of no use.
Life's span dwindles day and night,
Exert effort while time allows,
The worldly truths are impermanent,
Do not be deluded and fall into darkness.
One should learn to light the lamp of intent,
cultivate oneself to seek wisdom,
stay pure and avoid defilement,
hold the torch to observe the path of enlightenment.
The Chapter on Cherishing Oneself,
is intended to encourage learning,
which ultimately benefits oneself—
by eradicating sins and cultivating blessings.
"Those who love themselves,
guard carefully what they preserve,
yearn for liberation from desires,
study righteousness and do not slumber.
To cultivate oneself is of foremost importance,
always strive to learn diligently,
benefit others by imparting knowledge,
without weariness, wisdom will be attained.
First learn to rectify oneself,
then rectify others;
cultivate the body to enter wisdom,
and prioritize transformation through migration.
If one cannot benefit oneself,
how can one benefit others?
With a harmonious mind and upright body,
what wish remains unfulfilled?
What I have created myself,
I later experience myself;
the evil I do returns to me,
like a diamond drilling into a pearl.
If one does not uphold precepts,
they spread like vines,
indulging in unrestrained desires,
and evil deeds increase daily.
Evil deeds endanger one's self,
yet the foolish consider them easy;
Goodness best secures one's well-being,
but the foolish regard it as difficult.
As the Perfected One teaches,
embodying the Way through its principles,
the ignorant resent it,
and upon seeing it, regard it as evil.
Doing evil brings evil,
like planting bitter seeds,
evil bears its own punishment,
goodness reaps its own blessings,
each must ripen in its turn,
none can substitute for another;
practicing goodness yields goodness,
just as planting sweet crops.
Benefiting oneself and others,
Giving advantage without cost,
If you wish to know how to benefit yourself,
Heeding admonitions is the foremost way.
If one has personal worries,
desires rebirth in the heavens,
reverently delights in hearing the Dharma,
should contemplate the Buddha's teachings."
"In all actions, one must plan ahead,
lest they harm essential duties;
thus, the mind daily refines itself,
and affairs never miss their timing."
Those who govern affairs,
can achieve success and benefit in the end,
truly seeing themselves as they ought to act,
thus obtain what they desire.
The Chapter on the Mundane World,
speaks of the world as an illusion and a dream,
urging one to abandon vanity and superficiality,
and strive to cultivate the practice of the Way.
Like a carriage on the road,
abandoning the broad and level path
to take a crooked byway invites ruin,
bringing the worry of a broken axle.
Departing from the law in this way,
one increases through wrongdoing,
the foolish cling to it until death,
and there will also be calamities to suffer.
Follow the righteous path,
do not pursue wicked deeds,
and you will live, dwell, and rest in peace,
free from calamities through all generations.
All things are like bubbles,
thoughts are like wild horses,
dwelling in the world is but an illusion—
why then delight in this?
If one can cut this off,
fell its root,
and do so day and night,
one will surely attain concentration.
One who gives with faith,
like a joyful person,
may follow a troubled mind,
and offer food to the multitude.
Such people day and night,
cannot attain settled mindfulness.
The worldly lack insight,
none perceive the truth of the Way.
As if glimpsing a faint light,
one should nurture good intentions.
Like geese flocking together,
they avoid snares and soar high.
The wise guide the world,
liberating the misguided masses.
All in the world must die,
there is no safety in the three realms,
though the heavens are joyful,
when blessings are exhausted, they too perish.
Observing all in the world,
no life is without end,
to escape the cycle of life and death,
one should practice the true path.
Delusion shrouds the world,
Greed blinds the sight,
Doubt rejects the path,
Suffering follows folly.
One dharma transcends faults,
referring to a deceitful person,
who cannot escape the afterlife,
and no evil is left uncommitted.
Though one may amass many treasures,
Piling them high as Mount Sōnggāo to the heavens,
Even if such wealth fills the entire world,
It is not as good as beholding the path's trace.
The unwholesome appears as wholesome,
Attachment seems like non-attachment,
Taking suffering for pleasure,
Is what the deluded person detests.
Fǎ Jù Jīng, Scroll One
Where the Buddha resided,
they thoroughly expounded his teachings.
Thereafter, the five schools
of monks each extracted verses of four lines
or six lines from the collected scriptures,
arranging them by meaning and categorizing them into chapters.
They meticulously considered all twelve divisions of the scriptures,
finding no specific name for it,
thus calling it "Fǎ Jù" (Dharma Verses).
The scriptures are the words of the Dharma;
"Fǎ Jù" means
derived from the Dharma's words.
In recent times, a scholar named Gé compiled seven hundred verses;
their meanings were profoundly profound,
yet the translators rendered them rather obscurely.
The Buddha is hard to encounter,
his texts difficult to hear;
moreover, all Buddhas arose in Tiānzhú (India),
where the language differs in sound from Hàn Chinese.
It is said their writing is celestial script,
their speech celestial language;
with names and things being different,
transmitting the truth is truly not easy.
Only in the past, the Marquis of Lándiào'ān, Shì Gāo,
and the Commandant Fó Tiáo,
translated Sanskrit into Chinese,
truly capturing its essence,
a feat already hard to match.
Later translators,
though unable to achieve such precision,
still often valued their treasures,
roughly grasping the main ideas.
Initially, Wei Zhínán,
who hailed from India,
arrived in Wǔchāng in the third year of the Huángwǔ era,
and I received from him these five hundred gāthās,
requesting his companion Zhú Jiāngyàn to translate them.
Although Jiāngyàn was proficient in the Indian language,
he had not fully mastered Chinese,
so his translations
sometimes captured the Sanskrit terms directly,
or conveyed meanings through approximate sounds,
remaining plain and unadorned.
At first, I found the wording inelegant,
but Wei Zhínán said:
"The Buddha taught:
'Follow the meaning without embellishment,
and adopt the Dharma without adornment.'
The purpose of transmitting scriptures is to make them easily understood,
without losing their original meaning—
that is what makes a translation good."
All present agreed:
"Lǎozǐ stated:
'Fine words are not truthful,
truthful words are not fine.'
Confucius also said:
'Writing cannot fully express speech,
nor speech fully convey thought.'
The sages' ideas are profound and boundless;
thus in translating Sanskrit meanings,
clarity and accuracy are truly essential."
Therefore, from the gāthās as conveyed by the translator,
we adhered to the original intent without literary polish,
omitting whatever was not understood in translation,
so there are many omissions and incomplete passages.
Yet although the wording is plain, the meaning is deep;
the text is concise but the teachings extensive,
connecting with numerous scriptures,
each chapter having core verses
and explanatory passages.
In India,
beginners who do not study the Dhammapada
are considered to have skipped the proper sequence.
It serves as the fundamental guide for novices
and the profound treasury for advanced practitioners,
capable of enlightening the ignorant,
resolving doubts,
and inspiring self-reliance in others.
Its study requires modest effort yet encompasses broad wisdom,
truly making it a subtle and essential teaching.
In the past when this scripture was transmitted,
there were parts that were not understood,
and when Jiāng Yàn arrived,
I further consulted him for clarification.
Receiving these verses,
I obtained thirteen additional chapters,
and by collating them with ancient texts,
made certain additions and revisions,
organizing the chapter sequence to form one volume of thirty-nine chapters in total,
comprising seven hundred and fifty-two verses altogether,
hoping this may be of benefit,
for all to broaden their inquiry together.
The Dhammapada, Lower Scroll
Composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta
Translated by Wu-era Tianzhu monk Vighna and others
The Chapter on Expounding the Buddha,
speaks of the Buddha's divine virtues,
all of which benefit and liberate,
illuminating as the world's standard.
Having conquered oneself, one does not receive evil,
One surpasses all in the world,
With vast and boundless wisdom,
Enlightening the deluded to enter the path.
Breaking free from the web without any hindrance,
Exhausting love with nothing accumulated,
The Buddha's intent is profound and boundless,
Guiding those who haven't walked the path to tread it.
The brave and steadfast establish a single mind,
Renouncing home, day and night they diminish,
Cutting off the roots, free from desires and thoughts,
Studying the right path, mindful and clear.
Seeing the truth, pure and without defilement,
Having crossed the abyss of the five realms,
The Buddha arises, illuminating the world,
To dispel all sorrows and sufferings.
It is difficult to attain human birth,
and rare to obtain a long life;
the appearance of a Buddha in the world is scarce,
and hearing the Dharma is equally hard to encounter.
I have neither refuge nor protection,
Nor do I have any companions;
Through accumulating one practice to attain Buddhahood,
Naturally, I penetrate the sacred path.
A shipmaster can ferry across waters,
vigor serves as the bridge.
People are bound by their lineages,
the one who crosses is the mighty hero.
One who destroys evil becomes a Buddha,
One who abides in the earth becomes a Brahmin,
One who eliminates hunger learns the Dharma,
One who severs lineage becomes a disciple.
Observing conduct and patience is foremost,
The Buddha speaks of Nirvana as the ultimate,
Abandon wrongdoing and become a monastic,
Do not harass or harm others.
Neither seduced nor angered,
Upholding all precepts completely,
Eating little, forsaking bodily desires, [04)Dwelling in secluded and hidden places.
With focused mind and possessing wisdom,
One is capable of honoring the Buddha's teachings.
Refrain from all evil,
Embrace all good,
Purify your mind,
This is the teaching of the Buddhas.
The Buddha is the most venerable,
free from defilements and desires,
the mightiest among the Śākyas,
leading the multitude with a compassionate heart.
How delightful is the blessed reward,
where every wish is fulfilled,
swiftly reaching the ultimate tranquility,
and attaining Nirvana on one's own.
Some may turn to them on their own,
to the mountain and river spirits, the tree deities,
erecting temples and setting up images,
offering sacrifices and praying for blessings;
Since returning is like this,
neither auspicious nor supreme,
they cannot come,
to deliver me from all sufferings.
If there is one who returns of their own accord,
to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha,
the Path, the Virtue, and the Four Noble Truths,
they will surely behold the right wisdom.
Life and death are extreme suffering,
From the truths one attains liberation,
The eightfold path for transcending the world,
This removes all sufferings.
Since taking refuge in the Three Jewels,
It is the most auspicious and supreme,
Only this exists,
That liberates from all suffering.
A scholar who is upright and just,
devoted to the Way without stinginess,
how beneficial! Such a person,
naturally turns to the Buddha.
It is rare to encounter an enlightened person,
nor are they commonly found;
in the place where they are born,
their clan and relatives receive blessings.
The arising of all Buddhas brings joy,
The preaching of sutras brings joy,
The gathering of the multitude in harmony brings joy,
Harmony then brings constant peace.
Distinguish the safe from the perilous,
abandon evil and embrace goodness,
be swift yet not negligent.
My life is already at peace,
Not angered by grievances,
Though others hold grudges,
My actions bear no resentment;
I live in peace,
unafflicted by ailments,
while others suffer from illness,
my path remains free of malady;
My life is already at peace,
I am not troubled by worries,
While others have anxieties,
My path is free from sorrow.
My life is already at peace,
pure and effortless,
sustained by joy,
like the Ābhāsvara devas.
My life is already at peace,
serene and without troubles,
even if the nation's fire ignites a pile of firewood,
how could it burn me?
Victory breeds resentment,
defeat fosters self-contempt.
Abandon the mindset of winning and losing,
and peace follows without contention.
No heat surpasses lust,
no poison surpasses anger,
no suffering surpasses the body,
no joy surpasses extinction.
Without joy, with little joy,
with petty arguments, with small wisdom,
one who seeks the greater,
shall attain great peace.
I am the World-Honored One,
long freed from sorrows,
rightly guiding through the three realms of existence,
alone subduing all demons.
Seeing the sage is delightful,
gaining reliance is delightful,
escaping from fools is delightful,
practicing goodness alone is delightful.
Adhering to the right path brings joy,
mastering the art of speech brings joy,
and being free from disputes with the world;
maintaining complete precepts constantly brings joy,
Living alongside the virtuous brings joy,
As if reuniting with dear family,
Drawing near to the wise and benevolent,
Broadens knowledge and elevates aspirations.
Life's span is brief and few,
Yet many forsake the world anew.
In learning, grasp the essence true,
To ensure peace in age's view.
Those who wish to obtain the nectar,
Abandon desires and extinguish the truth of suffering swiftly,
Wishing to cross over the suffering of birth and death,
Should partake of the taste of nectar.
Those who are fond of pleasures,
restrain others from having many desires,
if they can avoid greed and lust,
then they will have no worries or calamities.
To deviate from the Way is to follow one's own inclinations,
while to follow the Way is to go against them.
Abandoning righteousness to pursue personal desires
is to yield to one's cravings.
Do not chase after what you love,
nor have what you dislike,
for seeing what you love brings no sorrow,
and seeing what you dislike also brings sorrow;
Thus, do not create attachment,
For attachment and aversion arise from it.
One who has already removed the bonds and fetters,
Has no attachment and thus nothing to detest.
Love and delight give rise to sorrow,
love and delight give rise to fear;
where there is no love or delight,
what sorrow? What fear?
Delight breeds sorrow,
delight breeds fear;
with no delight to cling to,
what sorrow? What fear?
Desire gives rise to sorrow,
desire gives rise to fear;
free from desire,
what sorrow? what fear?
Greed is restrained by precepts,
sincerity brings forth shame,
one's conduct aligns with the Way,
and thus is cherished by all.
Desires and appearances do not emerge,
thoughts become upright and then words are spoken,
the mind is free from greed and attachment,
one is sure to cut off the stream and cross over.
It is like a person who has been traveling for a long time,
returning safely from afar,
with all loved ones secure and well,
coming home with joy.
Those who are fond of doing good deeds,
travel from here to there,
reap blessings for themselves,
as if joy has come in person.
Rising from the sacred teachings,
restraining what is unwholesome,
drawing near to the Way brings clarity and affection,
while straying from it fosters no kinship.
Whether near or not near,
the dwellings differ;
near the Way, one ascends to heaven,
not near, one falls into hell.
The Chapter on Anger,
Shows how hatred and malice cause harm,
While tolerance, kindness, and gentleness,
Bring divine protection and human affection.
Anger does not see the Dharma,
Anger does not know the Way,
One who can eliminate anger,
Has blessings and joy always following them.
Greed and lust obscure the Dharma,
So does a foolish and ignorant mind.
Those who rid themselves of lust and folly,
Attain the foremost and supreme blessing.
To be able to restrain one's anger,
like stopping a runaway chariot,
is to be a skilled charioteer,
abandoning darkness and entering the light.
Endurance overcomes wrath,
Goodness overcomes evil,
The victorious are capable of giving,
Sincerity overcomes deceit.
Do not deceive, do not be wrathful,
desires are not excessive,
these three things,
upon death, one ascends to heaven.
Always maintaining self-discipline,
with a compassionate heart that refrains from killing,
one is thus reborn in heaven,
arriving there without sorrow.
With constant awareness in thought,
one diligently pursues learning with clarity and admiration,
until all defilements are exhausted and the mind is liberated,
leading to the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
People slander and defame one another,
from ancient times to the present day.
They criticize those who are too talkative,
and also disparage those who are silent and tolerant.
Even the moderate and harmonious are not spared from blame.
In this world, no one escapes being slandered.
To harbor intentions contrary to the sages,
one cannot maintain balance.
Each criticism and each praise,
merely serves personal gain and reputation.
The wise praise only those who are virtuous.
They commend solely the worthy.
The intelligent uphold precepts,
leaving no room for reproach or slander.
Like the purity of an Arhat,
Do not slander falsely.
All people praise,
Praised by Brahmā and Śakra,
Constantly maintain vigilance over oneself,
to guard against anger and resentment;
eliminate evil deeds of the body,
and advance in cultivating virtuous conduct,
Constantly guard careful speech,
to protect against anger and resentment;
Eliminate malicious words from the mouth,
recite and practice the teachings of the Dharma,
Constantly maintain a cautious mind,
to guard against anger and resentment.
Eliminate evil thoughts from the heart,
and contemplate the path of mindfulness.
Restrain your body and guard your speech,
keep control over your mind.
Abandon anger and practice the Way,
forbearance is the greatest strength;
Abandon anger and forsake arrogance,
Avoid all gatherings of desire.
Do not cling to name and form,
Through non-action, extinguish suffering.
Rising to dispel anger,
lust naturally ceases.
Abandoning unclear vigor,
thus all attain peace,
With anger severed, one rests in peace;
With resentment quelled, lust and sorrow cease.
Rage is the root of venom's might,
Gentle thoughts, the Brahmin's light.
Words of goodness earn renown,
Severance brings no trouble down.
Comrades draw close,
yet meticulously engage in wrongdoing,
later parting leaves lingering resentment,
fire consumes them with self-inflicted torment.
Unaware of shame,
without precepts yet harboring anger,
dragged by this anger,
unwearyingly engaged in affairs.
Strength leans towards force,
weakness towards softness,
yet forbearance stands supreme,
thus one should always endure frailty.
When the masses belittle you,
the strong endure,
for endurance is supreme,
one should always endure weakness.
Between myself and others,
There are three great fears;
If aware of their actions,
One should quell them within oneself.
Both practice righteousness,
I follow his teachings,
as if knowing his actions,
one should extinguish the self within.
The bitter wisdom surpasses folly,
coarse words and harsh speech,
one who desires constant victory,
should remain silent in speech.
Those who commit evil deeds,
will face the consequences of their anger,
whether or not anger is repaid with anger,
victory over them will defeat their aggression.
The Chapter on Dust and Grime,
distinguishes purity from filth,
urging learning to be immaculate,
and conduct to be without stain or disgrace.
Living without virtuous deeds,
one falls into evil paths upon death,
dwelling in swift and uninterrupted suffering,
arriving destitute without resources.
One should seek wisdom,
to make the mind steadfast,
remove defilements without staining,
and thus may depart from the form of suffering.
The wise person progresses gradually,
Peacefully and steadily advancing bit by bit,
Washing away the impurities of the mind,
As a craftsman refines gold.
Evil arises from the heart,
and in turn corrupts one's own form,
just as iron develops rust,
which eventually consumes the iron itself.
Not reciting is the stain of speech,
not diligent is the stain of the household,
not stern is the stain of complexion,
heedlessness is the stain of affairs,
Stinginess is the stain of generosity,
unwholesomeness is the stain of conduct,
in this life and the next,
evil dharmas are the perpetual stain.
Of all impurities within impurities,
None is greater than ignorance.
Learning should abandon evil,
Thus a monk becomes pure.
If one lives without shame,
like a bird with a long beak,
brazenly enduring disgrace,
it is called a filthy existence.
Though honesty and shame may bring hardship,
righteousness seeks purity,
avoiding disgrace without falsehood,
this is called a life of integrity.
The foolish are fond of killing,
Their words lack sincerity,
They take without giving,
And covet others' wives.
Indulging desires and violating precepts,
Bewildered by the intoxication of wine,
Such a person, life after life,
Undermines their own foundation.
If a person realizes this,
they should not entertain evil thoughts,
for foolishness draws near to wrongdoing,
and in time, it consumes them.
If one performs charity for the sake of faith,
desiring to enhance reputation,
gathering people with false pretenses,
that is not entering pure concentration.
To sever all desires,
cut off the root of the mind,
maintain single-mindedness day and night,
one will surely enter meditative concentration.
Storing filth becomes dust,
from stained dust it leaks,
unstained, it does not act,
purified and free from folly.
Seeing others' faults,
constantly reflect inwardly,
actions free from self-deception,
defilements exhausted without impurity.
No fire burns hotter than lust,
no arrow flies swifter than rage,
no net entangles tighter than folly,
love's torrent outruns the river's flow.
The void leaves no wheel tracks,
The monk harbors no external thoughts,
All people indulge in evil pleasures,
Only the Buddha is pure and untainted;
The void leaves no wheel tracks,
The monk has no outward thoughts,
All in the world is impermanent,
The Buddha has nothing of mine.
The chapter on upholding and maintaining,
explains the meaning of the teachings,
the Dharma values virtuous conduct,
and does not employ greed or extravagance.
Those who are devoted to the true path,
do not contend for profit,
whether there is gain or no gain,
they remain free from desire and unswayed.
Cháng Mǐn was fond of learning,
rectified his heart to act,
embraced treasured wisdom,
this is called practicing the Way.
The so-called wise person,
does not necessarily engage in eloquent debate;
free from fear and dread,
upholding goodness is wisdom.
One who upholds the Dharma,
does not rely on many words;
even if one has heard little,
but practices in accordance with the Dharma,
and does not forget to abide by the path,
can be called a true upholder of the Dharma.
What is called old age
does not necessarily refer to advanced years,
mature form and white hair,
but rather to foolishness and ignorance;
He who cherishes the truth,
is gentle and benevolent in harmony,
clear-sighted and pure in conduct,
is called an elder.
What is called upright governance
is not about appearances as flowery as blossoms,
nor stinginess, jealousy, or false pretenses,
but rather avoiding contradictions in words and deeds;
To say one can abandon evil,
the root has already been severed,
wise and without anger,
this is true integrity.
What is called a śramaṇa,
does not necessarily mean shaving one's head;
deceitful speech and greedy grasping,
having desires like an ordinary person—
To be able to cease evil,
expand and uphold the great Way,
calm the mind and extinguish thoughts,
this is what it means to be a Shāmén.
So-called bhikkhus,
beg for food at improper times,
engage in illicit sexual conduct,
bearing the name alone;
To abandon sin and merit,
purely cultivate the ascetic practice,
with wisdom able to destroy evil,
this is a bhikṣu.
What is called benevolence and wisdom,
is not merely refraining from speaking,
nor just having an impure heart,
and outwardly conforming;
To say the mind is non-active,
internally practicing purity and emptiness,
this and that are extinguished in tranquility,
this is benevolence and clarity.
What is called having the Way,
is not about saving just one thing;
it is to universally aid all under heaven,
doing no harm is the Way.
Refrain from speaking to the multitude,
My actions are filled with sincerity.
To attain a focused mind,
One must practice restraint and frugality.
Seeking peace through understanding.
Do not emulate ordinary people,
For they have not severed their attachments,
And thus cannot attain liberation.
The Chapter on Practicing the Way,
aims to expound the essential principles
of the path to liberation,
which is the most sublime.
The eightfold path is the supreme way,
the four truths are the footprints of the Dharma.
Abstaining from lust is the noblest conduct,
offering lamps surely brings the eye of wisdom.
This path holds no more fear,
Seeing purity leads to liberation in the world,
This can destroy the armies of demons,
Striving diligently extinguishes evil and suffering.
I have opened the right path,
revealing great wonders and illumination,
having heard it, one should practice it oneself,
for practice unties the bonds of falsehood.
Birth and death are constant sufferings,
To perceive this is wisdom,
Wishing to leave behind all sufferings,
Practice the path and all will be dispelled;
Life and death are not eternal emptiness,
To observe and perceive is wisdom,
If one wishes to be free from all suffering,
They should diligently practice the Way.
Rise when it is time to rise,
Do not be foolish and sink into the abyss,
Do not gaze upon the gathering of the fallen,
For schemes that cease will not advance the Way.
If one contemplates what should be contemplated, it is righteous;
if one contemplates what should not be contemplated, it is wicked;
with wisdom and without giving rise to wickedness,
by thinking of the right path, one achieves success.
Guard your words and hold fast to your thoughts,
Do not act upon what is unwholesome in body,
Thus, by eliminating these three actions,
The Buddha declares this is the attainment of the Way.
Cut down a tree without felling its root,
the roots remain and it will sprout again.
Only when the root is removed is there no tree,
so a monk attains Nirvana.
Unable to sever attachments,
relatives cling to each other,
bound by their own greedy desires,
like a calf yearning for milk;
To sever the root of the mind,
The cycle of birth and death becomes boundless no more,
This is the path to draw near,
Swiftly attaining Nirvana.
Greed and lust lead to aging,
anger and resentment cause illness,
ignorance and delusion bring death,
eliminate these three to attain the Way.
Releasing the past and understanding the future,
Freeing oneself from the middle and transcending the other,
All thoughts extinguished,
No more aging and death.
When one's wife and children are in the camp,
Without observing the methods of treating illness,
Sudden death arrives swiftly,
Like a torrent of water rushing abruptly.
If father and son do not save each other,
what hope is there for other relatives?
Life depends entirely on relying on one's kin,
like a blind man guarding a lamp.
Understand this meaning with wisdom,
you may cultivate the scriptures and precepts,
diligently practice to transcend the world,
and eliminate all suffering.
Stay away from all abysses,
like the wind dispelling clouds,
having extinguished thoughts,
this is called true knowledge.
Wisdom stands as the eternal guide for the world,
Serene joy arises from non-action,
Understanding and embracing the true teachings,
One brings an end to the cycle of life and death.
Knowing the multitude's actions are empty,
this is called wise insight;
ceasing to loathe the sufferings of the world,
from this path they are removed.
Knowing the multitude of sufferings in existence,
this is called wise insight;
being weary and disgusted with the sufferings of the world,
one eliminates them through this path.
All actions are not the self,
this is called wise insight,
cease to loathe the sufferings of the world,
and from this path, they are removed.
I speak to you the Dharma,
shoot with the arrow of love,
you should exhort yourself,
and accept the Tathāgata's words.
I have established the capital to extinguish,
Coming and going, life and death are exhausted,
Not by a single emotion to be understood,
What is expounded becomes the eye of the Way.
The swift current flows into the sea,
Torrents surge and swiftly fill,
Thus for the wise it is taught,
One may partake of sweet dew.
Never before had the Dharma wheel been heard,
Turning out of compassion for all beings,
Thus, those who serve it devoutly,
Pay homage to transcend the three realms of existence.
Three thoughts can lead to goodness,
three can also foster unwholesomeness;
from thoughts arise actions,
to extinguish them is the right endeavor.
Three determinations turn thoughts,
Abandon attachments, act boundlessly,
Attain three-three burrows removed,
Untie knots, respond with mindfulness.
Knowing to use precepts to guard against evil,
Contemplating the joy of wisdom and mindfulness,
Having understood the world's successes and failures,
One calms the mind and attains complete liberation.
The Chapter on Widespread Extension,
speaks of how all good and evil,
