accumulate from small to great,
as evidenced in the verses.
Though the charity is small,
its reward is vast;
wisdom from a modest offering,
receives evident blessings.
To impose toil upon others,
yet hope for divine favor,
brings calamity and blame upon oneself,
inviting widespread resentment.
Already engaged in many affairs,
they also create matters where none exist,
indulging in music and revelry,
their bad habits increasing daily.
Diligence is the only practice,
learning what is right and discarding what is wrong,
cultivating oneself to attain self-awareness,
this is the correct learning.
Being naturally intelligent and wise,
and also extensively learned,
he gradually advanced to become universally knowledgeable,
like butter blending smoothly into water.
Lacking wisdom and intent,
disinclined to learning and inquiry,
narrow-minded and constricted,
like cheese dissolving in water.
The Way that is near appears bright and clear,
like the snow on a high mountain;
the Way that is distant seems dark and obscure,
like an arrow shot at night.
As disciples of the Buddha,
we should constantly awaken and be self-aware,
chanting the Buddha's name day and night,
contemplating the Dharma and reflecting on the Sangha;
As disciples of the Buddha,
one should awaken to self-awareness,
contemplate meditation at day's end,
and delight in observing a unified mind.
One should maintain mindful intention,
knowing to eat less with each meal,
thus desiring to reduce suffering,
moderating consumption to preserve longevity.
Learning is difficult, abandoning faults is difficult,
living at home is also difficult,
gathering and sharing benefits is difficult,
but nothing surpasses the difficulty of existence.
It's hard for a monk to beg,
How can one not strive on their own?
Through diligence, one attains natural ease,
And later, desires nothing from others.
With faith, precepts are perfected;
From precepts, treasures are often obtained;
Also from them, harmony is attained,
And wherever one goes, offerings are sustained.
Sitting in one place, lying in one spot,
walking without indulgence,
maintaining unity to rectify oneself,
the heart delights in dwelling among the trees.
The Chapter on Hell,
speaks of the affairs of Nìlì,
where doing evil leads to receiving evil,
and the pull of sin does not cease.
The hell for false speech is near,
Claiming what was done as undone,
Both offenses will be suffered later,
This conduct drags one there by oneself.
With the robe upon his body,
He cannot restrain himself from evil deeds;
If one indulges in wicked conduct,
In the end, he will fall into hell.
If one without precepts receives offerings,
Is it not self-destructive in principle?
In death, they devour burning iron balls,
Burning fiercely, more intense than fiery coals.
There are four matters of indulgence:
being prone to violate others' women,
lying in peril brings no welfare,
third is slander, fourth is lewdness and debauchery.
Not benefiting leads to falling into evil,
Fearing evil, fearing scant joy,
The king's law imposes heavy punishments,
Upon death, one enters hell.
Just as pulling up sedge grass,
if you grasp it loosely, you'll hurt your hand;
so in learning precepts without restraint,
the prison's record will bring self-harm.
One who acts sluggishly,
Unable to rid others of toil,
With flaws in their spiritual practice,
Will never receive great blessings.
Always practice what should be practiced,
Strengthen self-discipline with determination,
Stay away from all heretical paths,
Do not learn what defiles like dust.
Engaging in what should not be done,
then leads to the accumulation of pent-up toxicity.
Practicing good deeds often brings auspiciousness and smoothness,
so that wherever one goes, there is no regret or remorse.
As for the multitude of evil deeds,
whether intended or already committed,
they bring suffering that cannot be undone,
and the guilt is near, hard to evade.
Falsely accusing to seek victory,
Conducting oneself with impropriety,
Resenting and slandering the virtuous,
Thereby wronging the principled scholars.
Crimes bind such a person,
Who casts themselves into a pit.
As if guarding a border fortress,
firmly secured both inside and out.
Guard your own mind,
so that no unwholesome thoughts arise;
moral failings lead to distress,
causing one to fall into hell.
What should be shameful is not shameful,
What is not shameful is instead shameful,
In life, one holds heretical views,
In death, one falls into hell;
To fear not what should be feared,
but to fear what should not be feared,
believing in wrong views,
leads to falling into hell upon death.
Avoiding what should be avoided,
embracing what should be embraced,
indulging in heretical views,
one falls into hell upon death;
drawing near what should be drawn near,
distancing from what should be distanced,
constantly upholding right views,
one ascends to a favorable path upon death.
The Chapter on Similes and Parables,
teaches people to correct their conduct,
for doing good leads to good,
and the reward of blessings brings joy.
I am like an elephant in battle,
unafraid of arrows in the midst,
always acting with sincerity and trust,
thus having no need to guard against others.
Just as an elephant is tamed and trained,
it becomes fit for a king's mount;
so when one's character is refined to become honorable,
then they receive trust and sincerity.
Although it is a common tune,
like those newly galloping,
it may be the best imitation,
yet it is not as good as self-adjustment.
Those who cannot adapt,
cannot reach where others do not go.
Only those who master self-adjustment,
can attain the method of adjustment.
Just as an elephant named Wealth Guard,
Violent and harmful, hard to restrain,
Tethered and deprived of food,
Still runs wild and breaks free.
Those who are immersed in evil deeds,
are constantly bound by their own greed,
like an elephant unaware of satiety,
thus repeatedly enter the womb.
Originally intending pure conduct,
and always acting with peace,
completely abandoning and subduing the fetters,
like a hook taming a wild elephant.
To delight in the Way without negligence,
And to constantly guard one's own mind,
Is to uproot the body's suffering,
Like an elephant freed from the mire.
If one gains a companion who is virtuous and capable,
Together they embark on deeds, firm in goodness and bold,
They can subdue all that is heard of vice,
And reach their goals without disappointment;
Without a virtuous companion by my side,
Together we'd tread paths wicked and defiant,
Widely severing the king's cities and lands,
How could I alone refrain from evil deeds?
It is better to do good alone,
than to keep company with fools;
to remain solitary and avoid evil,
like a wild elephant guarding itself.
To be born with benefits and ease is peace,
To accompany gentleness and harmony is peace,
To end one's life with fortune is peace,
To avoid all evils is peace.
One finds joy in having a mother,
And also joy in having a father;
There is joy in the world with monks,
And joy when the world follows the Way.
Upholding precepts brings peace in old age,
Believing in the right leads to true goodness,
Wisdom provides the safest refuge,
And abstaining from evil is the greatest peace.
Like a well-trained horse, gentle and supple,
it follows one's will wherever directed,
faithful in precepts and diligent in practice,
perfecting the essential methods of concentration.
With clarity in action and accomplishment,
endurance harmonizes and intention settles,
thus severing all sufferings,
following the heart's desires wherever they lead.
From this point onward, one attains stability,
like a well-trained horse,
cutting off anger and free from defilements,
thus receiving heavenly bliss.
Without self-indulgence,
from this comes frequent awakening,
comparing a lean horse to a fine one,
abandoning evil to become virtuous.
The Chapter on Love and Desire,
disdains lewdness and affection,
for which worldly people,
greatly generate calamities and harm.
When the mind indulges in lewd conduct,
desires and attachments grow like branches,
spreading and flourishing abundantly,
leaping beyond even the greedy fruit-eating monkey.
Thinking that love endures suffering,
Greed and desire cling to the world,
Worries and troubles grow day and night,
Spreading like the growth of creeping vines.
People are deluded by affection and love,
Unable to abandon passions and desires.
Thus, worries and attachments abound,
Flowing ceaselessly, filling the pond.
The reason for sorrow and grief,
The sufferings of the world are not one alone,
But they arise because of attachment;
Without attachment, there is no sorrow.
How can one abandon worries with a settled mind?
Without love, what remains in this world?
Without worries, one seeks not to be tainted,
Without love, how can peace be attained?
When there is sorrow leading to death at times,
It often brings many relatives together,
Embarking on the long journey of sorrow,
Where love and suffering often lead to peril.
One who practices the Way,
does not associate with desires,
first eliminates the root of attachment,
so that it has nowhere to take root.
Do not be like cutting reeds,
allowing the mind to grow again.
Like a tree with deep and firm roots,
even if cut down, it will grow back again;
if the attachments of desire are not completely eradicated,
one will repeatedly return to suffer.
The ape, once freed from the tree,
Escapes only to return to it.
So too are the multitudes—
They leave prison only to enter it again.
Greed and desire become the constant flow,
Habitually mingled with arrogance and pride,
Thoughts linger on lustful desires,
Self-blinded, they see nothing.
All streams of thought proliferate,
Entwined by attachments like creeping vines.
Only through the discerning insight of wisdom
Can the root of the mind be severed.
From affection comes moistening grace,
Thoughts grow and spread in every place,
Desires run deep, an endless sea,
Hence aging and death multiply endlessly.
The branches of existence never cease,
Yet one indulges in greed and desire,
Nourishing resentment, swelling the burial mound,
The foolish are ever restless and anxious.
Though a prison has hooks and chains,
The wise do not call it a true confinement;
Foolish views of wife and children as solace
Breed attachment—love is the firmest prison.
Wisdom says love is a prison,
deep-seated and hard to escape.
Therefore, one should sever and abandon it;
by not gazing upon desires, one can find peace.
Upon seeing beauty, the heart is deluded,
not considering the contemplation of impermanence,
the foolish deem it lovely and good—
how can they know it is not real?
Wrapping oneself in sensual pleasures,
Is like a silkworm spinning its cocoon.
The wise can cut off and abandon them,
Without a glance, they remove all sufferings.
Those whose minds indulge in laxity,
perceive impurity as purity in debauchery,
their affections and desires grow ever stronger,
and from this, they forge their own prison cells;
One who awakens the mind to eliminate lust,
should constantly contemplate the impurity of desires.
From this, one emerges from the prison of wrong views,
and can sever the affliction of aging and death.
Blinded by the web of desires,
shrouded by the veil of affections,
they bind themselves in the prison of indulgence,
like fish entering the trap's mouth.
Sought after by old age and death,
Like a calf seeking its mother's milk,
Depart from desires, extinguish the traces of craving,
Emerge from the net without any hindrance.
One who fully understands the path removes all bonds of imprisonment,
Resolving all conflicts between this and that,
Having crossed to the far shore, they walk on,
Such a one is called a great wise person.
Do not be intimate with those far from the Dharma,
Nor be bound by attachments and affections.
Those who fail to sever the three periods of time,
Will again fall into extreme paths.
If one perceives all dharmas,
And can refrain from clinging to any dharma,
All affections and understandings,
This is what it means to comprehend the sage's intent.
Among all gifts, the gift of the Dharma is supreme;
among all flavors, the flavor of the Dharma is supreme;
among all joys, the joy of the Dharma is supreme;
the extinction of craving conquers all sufferings.
Foolishly, I bind myself with greed,
Not seeking to cross to the other shore.
Because greed is a place of ruin,
It harms others and also harms oneself.
Desire and craving are the field,
lust, anger, and delusion are the seeds;
thus, those who give to the world
gain immeasurable blessings.
With abundant wealth but few companions,
The merchant trembles with fear and anxiety.
Greed and desire can harm one's life,
Thus wisdom lies in not coveting desires.
If the mind can be regulated, then desires are acceptable,
Why must one solely focus on the five desires?
If defiance can cut off the five desires,
That indeed makes one a warrior.
Without desires, one has no fears,
Serene and detached, free from worries and troubles.
To eliminate desires is to untie the knots,
This is the way to emerge from the abyss for long.
If you want me to know your origin,
Your existence arises from thought.
If I do not think of you,
Then you cease to be.
Cease felling trees abruptly,
for trees give rise to various evils;
cut down trees completely by the roots,
just as a bhikkhu attains Nirvana.
If one does not cut down the tree,
even a little more remains dear,
the heart is tied to it,
like a calf seeking its mother.
The Chapter on Material Gains encourages self-restraint to guard against greed, to reflect on virtue when seeing it, and not to lead a defiled life.
The banana plant dies for its fruit,
So too does the bamboo and reed.
The mule perishes from its pregnancy,
As a scholar ruins himself with greed.
Thus, greed brings no benefit,
Know it arises from folly's seed.
Fools, harming the virtuous for this,
Lie headless on the ground, deceased.
Though the heavens rain down the seven treasures,
desires remain insatiable,
joys are few and sorrows many,
the awakened are deemed virtuous.
Even with heavenly desires,
the wise forsake greed without attachment,
finding bliss in detachment from affection,
they become disciples of the Buddha.
Straying from the path, following the wicked,
greedy for support as a bhikṣu,
harboring only miserly thoughts,
offering them to other clans.
Do not rely on such sustenance,
forsake faults for the household,
this is not the ultimate intent,
what benefit comes from such use?
Fools devise foolish plans,
desires and arrogance multiply,
alas, they lose their advantage,
Nirvāṇa is not the same.
Those who truly know this,
bhikṣus, children of the Buddha,
do not delight in gains and offerings,
dwelling in solitude, they quell their thoughts.
Self-attained, they do not boast,
nor do they hope from others,
for those bhikṣus who hope,
do not reach true concentration.
To secure one's life,
calm the mind and reflect inwardly,
not calculating the measure,
of clothing and food;
to secure one's life,
calm the mind and reflect inwardly,
attain contentment with what is gained,
uphold the practice of one dharma;
to secure one's life,
calm the mind and reflect inwardly,
like a mouse hiding in its burrow,
secretly and humbly study the teachings.
Restrain profit and restrain the ears,
uphold precepts and contemplate,
praised by the wise,
pure and auspicious, do not be negligent.
As if possessing the three insights,
liberated and without outflows,
with scant wisdom and little knowledge,
having nothing to recollect.
Regarding food and drink,
gaining profit from others,
yet harboring evil dharmas,
envious of offerings received.
Entangled in much resentment and gain,
forcibly donning the dharma robe,
only hoping for food and drink,
not upholding the Buddha's teachings.
Know this as a fault,
sustenance is a great fear,
taking little brings no worry,
a bhikṣu's heart is released.
Without food, life cannot be sustained;
Who can refrain from seeking sustenance?
Thus, securing food is of foremost importance,
Knowing this, one should not harbor envy.
Jealousy first harms oneself,
Then it harms others.
To strike others invites being struck in return,
This cannot be avoided.
Better to chew on burning stones,
Or swallow molten copper,
Than to partake of the faithful offerings of others
Without moral discipline.
The Chapter on the Monastic,
instructed with the righteous Dharma,
disciples receive and practice it,
attaining the Way, liberated and purified.
Fix the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth,
the body and mind constantly abide in righteousness,
a bhikkhu who practices thus,
can be freed from all sufferings.
Do not recklessly harm with hands and feet,
Govern speech and align with actions,
Constantly find joy within, steady the mind,
Maintain single-mindedness in tranquility.
Learning should guard the tongue,
Speech should be calm and measured,
Based on the principles of righteousness,
Words must be gentle and soft.
Delighting in the Dharma, desiring the Dharma,
Contemplating the peaceful Dharma,
The bhikṣu abides by the Dharma,
Upright and without waste.
Learning without seeking profit,
without cherishing others' practices,
a monk who envies others
cannot attain concentration.
A monk takes little,
thus gaining without hoarding,
praised by gods and humans,
born pure and undefiled.
The bhikṣu practices compassion,
cherishes and reveres the Buddha's teachings,
penetrates deeply into śamatha and vipaśyanā,
and extinguishes karmic formations to attain peace.
All forms and names,
Do not cling to them, do not be deluded,
Not drawing near, not grieving,
Thus one becomes a monk.
A monk aboard a ship,
when empty becomes light;
rid of lust, anger, and delusion,
this is Nirvana.
Abandon the five and sever the five,
Contemplate the five faculties,
Be able to distinguish the five,
Then cross the river abyss.
Practice Chan without negligence,
Do not be disturbed by desires,
Lest you swallow molten copper,
Tormenting yourself and scorching your form.
Without meditation there is no wisdom,
without wisdom there is no meditation,
the Way comes from meditation and wisdom,
through which one attains Nirvana.
One should learn to enter emptiness,
dwell in stillness and restrain thoughts,
find joy in solitary seclusion,
and single-mindedly contemplate the Dharma.
Constantly restrain the five senses,
Subdue thoughts like still water,
Pure, serene, and harmonious,
Becomes the taste of sweet dew.
Not accepting all offerings,
being the wise monk Huì,
he restrains his senses and is content,
upholding all precepts and disciplines.
One should live a life of purity,
seek good teachers and friends,
for the wise help others grow,
crossing suffering to reach joy.
Like a withered flower,
ripe for its own fall,
abandon lust, anger, and delusion,
and liberation from birth and death will naturally unfold.
To cease the body and speech,
the mind abides in profound silence,
the bhikkhu renounces the world,
this is called embracing tranquility.
One should discipline oneself,
struggling inwardly with the heart,
guarding the body and contemplating truth,
thus the monk finds peace.
I exist for myself,
yet in strategy there is no self,
thus one should diminish the self,
and moderation makes one virtuous.
In Buddhism, joy is valued,
one may have abundant joy,
reaching even to solitude,
where actions cease and eternal peace abides.
If there is even a small practice,
following the Buddha's teachings and precepts,
this illuminates the world,
like the sun without clouds.
Abandon arrogance, leaving no trace of pride,
As the lotus flower blooms pure in water,
Learning to relinquish both this and that,
Know that such wisdom surpasses the old.
Cut off attachment without lingering affection,
Unattached like the lotus flower,
The bhikkhu crosses the river stream,
Triumphs over desires, illuminating the past.
To dam the flow by self-reliance,
To let the drifting heart renounce desires,
Benevolence does not sever desires,
Yet a single-minded intent still flees.
Do it! Do it!
You must force yourself to exercise restraint,
abandon your home and become lax,
yet your mind still becomes tainted again.
Those who act lazily and sluggishly,
how can their toilsome thoughts be dispelled?
Without pure and noble conduct,
how can one attain the great treasure?
What practice does a monk follow?
When the mind is unrestrained,
every step becomes entangled,
merely following wherever thoughts lead.
With the kasāya draped over the shoulders,
Committing evil without remorse,
Those who persist in wicked deeds
Shall fall into the evil paths.
Without discipline, it's hard to be admonished,
Like a tree withered by the wind,
Acting only for oneself,
Why not strive diligently?
To calm the mind is not about cutting away,
Negligence and deceit lack caution,
Abandon greed and contemplate the Way,
Then one should calm the mind;
To calm the mind without plucking it out,
To be unrestrained yet without faith,
One can extinguish all sufferings,
And become the foremost śramaṇa.
The Chapter on the Brahmin,
speaks of one whose conduct is pure,
whose learning is untainted,
worthy to be called a Daoist.
Crossing by damming the stream,
Desireless as a Brahmin,
With knowledge and conduct fully exhausted,
This is called a true Brahmin.
By the undivided Dharma,
one crosses the abyss purified,
with all desires and fetters resolved,
this is called a Brāhmaṇa;
Going where there is no 'other',
that 'other' is already void,
abandoning and renouncing lust,
this is called a Brahmin.
Pure in thought,
Faultless in action,
Not seeking rebirth above,
This is called a Brahmin.
The sun illuminates the day,
the moon illuminates the night,
armor and weapons illuminate the army,
meditation illuminates the Daoist;
the Buddha appears in the world,
illuminating all darkness.
Not by shaving one's head to become a śramaṇa,
nor by calling oneself a Brahmin,
can one be said to have abandoned all evils;
only thus is one a true practitioner.
He who renounces evil becomes a Brahmin,
He who enters the right path becomes an ascetic,
He who abandons my multitude of defiled actions,
This is indeed the renunciation of household life.
If one is attached to love,
the mind becomes unsettled;
having relinquished and corrected it,
this is the cessation of all sufferings.
One whose body, speech, and mind,
are pure and free from faults,
and who has abandoned the three actions,
is called a true Brahmin.
If the mind understands clearly,
the teachings spoken by the Buddha,
contemplate the mind and return to oneself,
purify through the practice of water.
Not by matted hair is one a Brahmin,
nor by lineage or birth;
he who is truthful and righteous,
pure and wise, is noble.
Adorning the hair without wisdom,
What use is a garment of grass?
If inwardly one does not detach from attachments,
What benefit is there in external renunciation?
Clad in worn-out robes,
personally upholding the practice of the Dharma,
dwelling in solitude and contemplation,
this is called a Brahmin;
The Buddha does not instruct others to do so,
yet praises himself and proclaims,
"As truthful and without falsehood,
thus is one a Brahmin."
Cut off all desires,
do not corrupt one's will,
abandon the multitude of wants,
this is called a Brahmin.
Severing the river of life and death,
able to endure and rise to cross over,
self-awakened and emerging from the abyss,
this is called a Brahmin;
When reviled and struck,
Silently enduring without anger,
Possessing the power of patience,
This is called a true Brahmin.
If one is wronged or cheated,
yet only thinks of upholding precepts,
rectifying oneself and practicing self-discipline,
this is called a true Brahmin.
One who abandons evil ways in heart,
like a snake shedding its skin,
untainted by desires,
is called a true Brahmin.
One who perceives life as suffering,
and from this extinguishes desire,
can lay down the heavy burden,
this is called a Brahmin;
One who comprehends subtle wisdom,
distinguishes the path from the non-path,
embodies and practices the highest righteousness,
is called a Brahmin.
Renouncing household life,
free from the fear of homelessness,
with few desires and minimal wants,
this is called a Brahmin.
Abandoning killing and giving life,
with no intention to harm,
causing no disturbance or annoyance,
this is called a Brahmin.
Avoid contention without contending,
bear offense without resentment,
respond to malice with kindness,
this is called a Brahmin's way;
To abandon lust, anger, and delusion,
pride, arrogance, and all evils,
like a snake shedding its skin,
this is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Severing worldly affairs,
uttering no harsh words,
examining the eight paths with discernment,
this is called a Brahmin;
Worldly evil dharmas,
whether long or short, great or small,
neither grasping nor rejecting,
this is called a Brahmin;
In this life, one's conduct is pure;
in the next life, there is no defilement.
Without attachments or rejections,
this is called a Brahmin.
Abandoning the self without reliance,
not reciting divergent practices,
practicing the extinction of sweet dew,
this is called a Brahmin;
Regarding sin and fortune,
both paths are forever eliminated,
free from worry, free from dust,
this is called a Brahmin;
With a heart joyful and unstained,
like the moon in full bloom,
slander and blame have been eradicated,
such is called a Brahmin.
Seeing the foolish come and go,
Falling into pits and suffering,
Wishing to cross the shore alone,
Not indulging in others' words,
Only extinguishing and not arising,
This is called a Brahmin.
Having severed affection and love,
leaving home without desires,
when all attachments are exhausted,
this is called a Brahmin.
Where people gather, yet one does not fall into celestial gatherings,
nor adhere to any assemblies,
unattached to all congregations,
this is called a true Brahmin.
Abandoning pleasures, having no pleasures,
Extinguishing what is without warmth or coolness,
Vigorously transcending all worlds,
This is called a Brahmin;
Having ended all births,
Death holds no destination for him,
Awakened and at peace, with no attachments,
This is called a Brahmin;
Having crossed the five paths,
None know where they fall,
Habits exhausted without remainder,
This is called a Brahmin;
Neither before nor after,
nor is there anything in between,
without grasping or renouncing,
this is called a Brahmin;
The mightiest, the bravest,
Who can liberate themselves,
With awakened mind unwavering,
Such is called a Brahmin.
Knowing one's own past lives,
the origins of one's comings and goings,
attaining the cessation of rebirth,
understanding the profound path with wisdom,
illuminating and capable of silence,
this is called a Brahmin.
Endurance is the supreme self-discipline,
Nirvana is praised by the Buddha as the highest state,
Renouncing home life without breaking precepts,
Quieting the mind causes no harm.
To be without illness is the greatest benefit,
To know contentment is the greatest wealth,
To have deep friendships is the greatest companionship,
Nirvana is the ultimate bliss;
Hunger is the gravest illness,
Karmic actions bring the greatest suffering,
Having truly understood this,
Nirvana is the greatest joy;
Few are those who go to the good path,
Many are those heading to the evil path,
If one truly understands this,
Nirvana is the greatest peace.
Good arises from causes,
Evil befalls from causes,
Nirvana too comes from causes,
And so do all conditioned phenomena.
As deer rely on the wilderness,
And birds rely on the sky,
The Dharma returns to its retribution,
The true person returns to extinction.
Does beginning exist or not?
Beginning neither exists nor doesn't exist,
This is the state of no attainment,
Where there is no thought either.
The mind is hard to perceive, but habits can be observed.
One who awakens to desires truly sees completely.
Where there is no joy, there lies the realm of suffering.
Being in craving and desire increases pain.
Clarity is not pure, yet purity can master it.
Having no attachments is the realm of suffering.
Seeing has its seeing, hearing has its hearing,
Thought has its thought, consciousness has its consciousness.
To perceive without attachment is also without consciousness.
Abandoning all is to reach the ultimate.
Eliminate thoughts of the body, cease the activities of sensation.
When consciousness is exhausted, suffering ends.
Resting leads to movement, emptiness leads to purity.
Movement is not near, nor does it hold joy.
Joy without attachment brings tranquility.
Tranquility becomes serene, having come and gone.
When coming and going cease, there is no birth or death.
With birth and death severed, there is no this or that.
When this and that are cut off, both are extinguished.
Extinction without remainder is the cessation of suffering.
The bhikṣu has worldly existence,
has being, has action and deeds,
yet there is non-arising without being,
without action and without deeds.
Only the thought-free one,
can attain self-realization,
non-arising without further being,
actionless and deedless.
Those with arising, being, action and deeds,
fail to grasp the essence;
if one understands non-arising,
non-being and non-action,
then arising and being attain the essence.
From arising and being having emerged,
action and deeds lead to mortal existence -
this reveals the fruit of Dharma.
From food as cause comes existence,
from food stem sorrow and joy;
but when this essence is extinguished,
no trace of thought remains.
All suffering is exhausted,
deeds ceased, serene and tranquil -
O bhikṣu, I have known:
no more entering any realm.
No entering emptiness,
no sensory realms employing entry,
no perception or non-perception entering,
no present world or future world,
nor even sun and moon concepts,
no going, nothing hanging.
I have no coming or going,
not departing nor arriving,
not sinking nor arising again -
this shore is Nirvāṇa.
Such form without form,
suffering and joy resolved,
what's seen no longer frightens,
wordless speech without doubt.
Sever existence's arrow,
avoid folly without attachment -
this is the supreme bliss,
this path, serene, unsurpassed.
Bear insult like the earth,
practice patience like a threshold,
pure as water without stain -
exhausted birth, no more receiving.
Victory brings no security,
though winning, suffering remains;
seek to abandon victory,
victory attained, nothing arises.
End the old, create not new,
disgusted with womb, no sensual acts;
seeds scorched, no more arising,
consciousness exhausted like fire extinguished.
Womb is a foul ocean -
why delight in sensual acts?
Though higher states exist,
none equal Nirvāṇa.
Know completely all is severed,
no more clinging to the world;
wholly abandon as extinction,
among paths, this is supreme.
Buddha reveals truth's Dharma,
wisdom and courage can uphold it;
practice pure, flawless,
self-knowing, crossing worlds in peace.
The path requires first renouncing desire,
early follow Buddha's precepts;
extinguish evil at evil's limit -
easy as bird vanishing in sky.
If understanding Dharma verses,
wholeheartedly embody the path's practice,
this crosses life-and-death's shore,
suffering ended without affliction.
Dharma has no close or distant,
rightness asks not weak or strong;
essential is no conceptual thought,
knots untied become pure.
The wise detest this rotting body,
perilous, fragile, unreal;
much suffering, little joy,
nine apertures, none pure.
Wisdom trades peril for safety,
abandons reliance, escapes all difficulties;
form decays, dissolves to foam,
wisdom sees, relinquishes greed.
See body as suffering's vessel,
birth, aging, sickness without pain;
abandon filth, practice purity,
may attain great peace.
Rely on wisdom to repel evil,
not receiving, exhaust defilements;
pure practice leads beyond world,
gods and humans all salute.
The Chapter on Life and Death explains that the souls of people, though their spirits depart, their consciousness remains, and they are reborn according to their deeds.
Life is like a fruit awaiting ripeness,
Often fearing it will wither and fall.
All that is born endures suffering,
Who can attain deathlessness?
From the start, delighting in affection and love,
One may sink into fleeting illusions,
Assuming a form, life is like lightning,
Flowing day and night, hard to halt.
This body is a mortal thing,
The spirit, an intangible essence;
Even if one dies and is reborn,
Deeds, good or evil, do not perish.
Endings and beginnings span not one lifetime,
Driven by ignorance and attachment, long they last;
From this, joy and sorrow arise,
The body dies, but the spirit does not fade.
The body, four elements form its matter,
Consciousness, four aggregates are called name;
Its aspects number eighteen kinds,
Conditioned by twelve links.
The spirit dwells in nine common abodes,
Birth and death do not cease,
The foolish in the world do not hear this,
Veiled in darkness, lacking the divine eye.
They smear themselves with three defilements,
Blind in mind, seeing falsely,
Some say death is like life,
Or claim death brings annihilation.
Consciousness creates the three realms,
Good and evil lead to five destinies,
Subtly moving, silently arriving,
Where it goes, like an echo responds.
In desire, form, and formless realms,
All stems from past deeds,
As seeds follow their original nature,
Naturally, retribution matches the intent.
The spirit takes the body as its name,
Like fire follows the form it burns,
Attached to a candle, it's candle fire,
Following charcoal, grass, or dung as fuel.
When mental factors arise, it arises,
When factors cease, it then ceases;
Rising and falling like rain or hail,
Revolving, unaware of itself.
Consciousness wanders the five paths,
No place it does not revisit,
Discarding one body, assuming another,
Like a wheel rolling on the ground.
As a person resides in one body,
Leaving an old dwelling behind,
The spirit uses form as its hut,
The form decays, but the spirit does not perish;
The spirit dwells in the physical frame,
Like a sparrow hidden in a vessel,
The vessel breaks, the sparrow flies away,
The body fails, the spirit departs to rebirth.
Nature, delusion, purity, eternal views,
Attachment to body, doubt, and false notions,
Discontent and longing are not the supreme essentials,
The Buddha declares these as ignorance.
One root, two unfoldings,
Three defilements, five expanding widely,
The oceans of existence, thirteen matters,
Abysses dissolve, crossing over brings joy.
When the three things are severed,
Know the body has no real worth,
Life breath, warmth, and consciousness,
Abandon the form and transmigrate.
When death lays it on the ground,
Like grass, devoid of awareness,
Observing its state thus,
Only illusion and foolish craving remain.
Those who benefit from the Way: the ruler, father, and teacher act by revealing the virtuous path, guiding with righteousness.
People know to serve their superiors,
Revering father, teacher, and the Way's masters,
Faith, precepts, charity, learning, and wisdom's light,
Bring auspicious ends and lives secure and bright.
Destined fate holds blessings and celebrations,
Born into the world as honored generations,
Using the Way to bring the world to peace,
All follow the Dharma without cease.
A king, as leader of subjects and folk,
With kindness and care, his rule bespoke,
Guiding by law and precept's way,
Showing fortune and misfortune's sway.
In safety, do not forget peril's threat,
With clear foresight, blessings grow yet,
The recompense of virtue and good deed,
Knows no distinction by rank or creed.
As a commander in this worldly sphere,
Uphold the right, free from crooked fear,
A mind subdued triumphs over vice,
Thus, one becomes a Dharma King, precise.
Seeing truth, bestowing benefits with grace,
Benevolent, loving, aiding the human race,
With fairness in benefits shared all around,
Thus, the masses gather, in loyalty bound.
Like an ox leading through water's flow,
Guide rightly, and followers rightly go,
Serving the Dharma with an upright heart,
Thus, all people find peace in every part.
Do not recklessly disturb the sacred sign,
Lest bitter pain and suffering entwine,
Malicious intent brings self-destruction near,
Never leading to a good sphere.
Virtue of precepts can be relied upon,
Blessings' reward follows like the dawn,
Upholding Dharma, one leads humankind,
Far from three evil paths, the mind aligned.
Precepts cautious, remove suffering and dread,
Virtue's blessings in three realms are spread,
Ghosts, dragons, evils, toxins, and harm,
Cannot touch those who keep precepts' charm.
Without righteousness, lacking sincere trust,
Deceit, falsehood, fond of conflict's thrust,
Know to stay far from such ways,
Near folly, sins in abundance blaze;
The kind and wise speak with honest word,
Learned, precepts kept, in accord,
Know to draw close and align,
Near wisdom, true goodness will shine.
Fine words without guarding the precept's vow,
A mind disordered, no good deeds allow,
Though dwelling in seclusion's hidden place,
This is not the Dharma-learning's grace.
Beautiful speech aligned with truth is best,
Dharma's discourse follows in the test,
Loving speech may rank as third,
Honest speech, no deceit, is heard.
Without cause, gaining a sharp blade's might,
One may use it to self-harm in plight,
Fools learning, fond of falsehood's tale,
Acts drag them to misfortune's jail.
Greed, lust, anger, and delusion's fire,
These three are not good's foundation, higher,
By these, the body brings self-harm,
Retribution springs from delusion's charm.
With blessings, one becomes deva or human being,
Without Dharma, evil forms are seeing,
Sages with clear, solitary sight,
Always well uphold the Buddha's light.
Precepts' virtue shapes future destiny,
Creating blessings that follow endlessly,
Devas and humans praise the good,
A heart upright, in peace has stood.
Doing evil without thought to cease,
Daily bound, no self-repentance's release,
Life passes like a river's flow,
This fear urges precepts to uphold and know.
Now I observe my head's crown,
White hairs appear, as if robbed by time's gown,
Already summoned by heaven's envoy call,
The time is right to leave it all.
The Chapter on Auspicious Omens concerns the art of self-cultivation, removing evil and embracing goodness, ultimately leading to abundant blessings and prosperity.
The Buddha honored passes through the heavens,
The Tathāgata often reveals the truth.
A Brahmin ascetic
Comes to ask, "What is auspicious?"
Then the Buddha, with compassion,
Explains the true essentials:
Having faith and delight in the true Dharma,
This is the most auspicious;
If not following celestial beings or humans,
Hoping for luck or chance,
Nor praying to deities in temples,
This is the most auspicious;
Befriending the virtuous and choosing a good dwelling,
Always prioritizing meritorious deeds,
Disciplining oneself to follow righteousness,
This is the most auspicious;
Abandoning evil and drawing near to good,
Avoiding alcohol and knowing self-restraint,
Not indulging in female charms,
This is the most auspicious;
Being learned and observing precepts,
Diligently studying the Dharma and discipline,
Cultivating oneself without contention,
This is the most auspicious;
Residing in filial piety, serving parents,
Managing the household, caring for wife and children,
Not engaging in empty actions,
This is the most auspicious;
Not arrogant, not self-important,
Content and mindful of cause and effect,
Reciting and studying scriptures timely,
This is the most auspicious;
Enduring what is heard with patience,
Eager to see monastic practitioners,
Listening and accepting whenever teachings are given,
This is the most auspicious;
Observing fasting and cultivating pure conduct,
Always desiring to see the noble and sage,
Relying on the wise,
This is the most auspicious;
Having faith in the virtuous,
With right intention and no doubt,
Wishing to escape the three evil paths,
This is the most auspicious;
With an impartial mind, practicing charity,
Honoring all who have attained the Way,
And respecting celestial beings and humans,
This is the most auspicious;
Always seeking to abandon greed and desire,
Ignorance, folly, and anger,
Able to learn the path of sincerity and insight,
This is the most auspicious;
If one discards wrongful pursuits,
And diligently cultivates the path's application,
Constantly engaging in what is worthy,
This is the most auspicious;
Acting for the sake of all under heaven,
Establishing great compassion,
Cultivating benevolence to comfort all beings,
This is the most auspicious.
To seek auspicious blessings,
One should believe in and revere the Buddha;
To seek auspicious blessings,
One should listen to the meaning of the Dharma verses;
To seek auspicious blessings,
One should make offerings to the Saṅgha.
Those with pure and complete precepts,
This is the most auspicious;
The wise dwelling in the world,
Constantly practice auspicious deeds,
Attaining wisdom and insight on their own,
This is the most auspicious.
The Brahmin, hearing the Buddha's teaching,
Felt great joy in his heart,
Stepped forward to bow at the Buddha's feet,
And took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
